linear_algebra.s: Vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, and least squares. Nearly every model in robotics is written in this language.
i: A matrix is a linear map: $Ax$ mixes the columns of $A$ weighted by the entries of $x$, so rank tells you how many independent directions the map can reach.
Eigenvalues of $A$ govern repeated application: $x_{k+1} = A x_k$ decays to zero exactly when every eigenvalue has magnitude less than 1.
When $Ax = b$ has no exact solution (more equations than unknowns), least squares picks $x$ minimizing $\|Ax - b\|^2$, given by the normal equations $A^\top A x = A^\top b$.
q: You fit a line to 50 noisy measurements by solving $Ax = b$ with $A$ of size $50 \times 2$. Why can't you just invert $A$?
$A$ is not square, so it has no inverse; least squares finds the $x$ that best fits all rows
$A$ is singular because the noise makes its columns linearly dependent on each other
Inversion works but is slower than least squares, which gives the same exact solution
The inverse exists but amplifies noise, so least squares discards half of the rows
A tall $50 \times 2$ matrix has no inverse and the overdetermined system generally has no exact solution; least squares minimizes the residual. Noise does not make the columns dependent.
linear_algebra.t: In NumPy, generate $y = 2t + 1$ plus noise for 50 points, build $A = [t,\ 1]$, and compare `np.linalg.lstsq(A, y)` with solving $A^\top A x = A^\top y$ directly.
linear_algebra.T:
Why a robotics course starts here

Almost everything in this course is written as vectors and matrices. A robot's state is a vector: a wheeled robot's pose is $x = (p_x, p_y, \theta)$. A model of how it moves, a controller, and a sensor's noise are all matrices acting on those vectors. You don't need the whole subject, just four ideas.

1. A matrix is a machine that moves vectors

Multiplying $A x$ takes the columns of $A$ and mixes them using the entries of $x$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = x_1 \begin{bmatrix} a \\ c \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} b \\ d \end{bmatrix}$$

So the columns of $A$ tell you where the axis directions land. That picture is what the first video above animates.

2. Solving $A x = b$

Asking "which $x$ produces $b$?" is solving $A x = b$. If $A$ is square and invertible, $x = A^{-1} b$. If $A$ squashes space flat (its rank is less than its size), some $b$ can never be reached, and that idea returns later as controllability.

3. Eigenvalues tell you what repeated steps do

Many robot models step forward in time as $x_{k+1} = A x_k$, so $x_k = A^k x_0$. An eigenvector $v$ is a direction that $A$ only stretches: $A v = \lambda v$. Along it, $k$ steps multiply by $\lambda^k$. If every eigenvalue has $|\lambda| < 1$, every state shrinks to zero; one eigenvalue with $|\lambda| > 1$ and some state blows up. That is the whole idea of stability for linear systems.

4. When there's no exact answer: least squares

With more equations than unknowns (say 100 noisy sensor readings, 3 unknowns), $A x = b$ usually has no solution. Least squares picks the $x$ that makes the error $\|A x - b\|^2$ smallest, given by the normal equations $A^\top A\, x = A^\top b$. Every estimator in Part III builds on this.

Worked example

Take $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}$. It is triangular, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: $\lambda_1 = 0.9$ and $\lambda_2 = 0.5$. Both have $|\lambda| < 1$, so $x_{k+1} = A x_k$ decays to zero from any start. The slow one, $0.9$, sets the pace: after 20 steps that part has shrunk to $0.9^{20} \approx 0.12$ of its size, while the $0.5$ part is essentially gone ($0.5^{20} \approx 10^{-6}$).

Common mistake: reading stability off the entries of $A$. A matrix can have small entries and still blow up, or big entries and still decay. Check the eigenvalues.

V.t: Linear transformations and matrices
Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

probability.s: Random variables, Bayes' rule, and the multivariate Gaussian. The book reviews these at the start of the estimation part, and they underpin every filter that follows.
i: Bayes' rule $p(x \mid z) = p(z \mid x)\, p(x) / p(z)$ turns a sensor model $p(z \mid x)$ and a prior $p(x)$ into a posterior belief; it is the core update step of every Bayes filter.

A multivariate Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ is fully described by its mean and covariance; $\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and its eigenvectors give the axes of the uncertainty ellipse.

Gaussians are closed under linear maps: if $x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ then $Ax + b \sim \mathcal{N}(A\mu + b,\ A\Sigma A^\top)$, which is why the Kalman filter can propagate beliefs exactly for linear systems.
q: A robot's 2D position belief has covariance $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1)$. It is transformed by $y = Ax$ with $A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 1)$. What is the new covariance?
$\operatorname{diag}(2, 1)$, because the covariance scales linearly with $A$
$\operatorname{diag}(4, 1)$, because covariance transforms as $A\Sigma A^\top$
$\operatorname{diag}(1, 1)$, because a linear map cannot change uncertainty
$\operatorname{diag}(0.5, 1)$, because stretching spreads probability thinner
Covariance transforms as $A\Sigma A^\top$, so variance along the first axis scales by $2^2 = 4$. Scaling by $A$ alone ($\operatorname{diag}(2, 1)$) confuses standard deviation with variance.
probability.t: Draw 10,000 samples from $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ in NumPy, multiply by $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, and compare `np.cov` of the result with $AA^\top$.
probability.T:
Why probability

A robot's sensors are noisy and its motion is never exact, so "where am I?" never has one certain answer. Probability is the language for "I'm probably here, possibly there". Everything in Part III of the course uses three ideas from it.

1. Bayes' rule: update a belief with evidence

You have a prior belief $p(x)$ about the state, and a sensor model $p(z \mid x)$: how likely reading $z$ is if the state is $x$. After seeing $z$, the updated belief, the posterior, is

$$p(x \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid x)\, p(x)}{p(z)}$$

The denominator $p(z)$ just makes the probabilities add up to one. In words: states that explain the reading well gain probability, states that don't lose it. This is exactly the correct step of the Bayes filter.

2. The Gaussian: a belief in two numbers

A Gaussian (normal distribution) $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is the bell curve: mean $\mu$ at the centre, standard deviation $\sigma$ setting the width. About 68% of the probability lies within $\pm\sigma$ of the mean and 95% within $\pm 2\sigma$. For a vector state it becomes $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$, where the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ holds each variable's variance on the diagonal and how they vary together off it. Its eigenvectors are the axes of the uncertainty ellipse.

3. Gaussians stay Gaussian

Two facts make Gaussians the workhorse of estimation:

  • A linear map keeps a Gaussian Gaussian. If $x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ then $Ax + b \sim \mathcal{N}(A\mu + b,\ A\Sigma A^\top)$. This is the Kalman filter's predict step.
  • Combining a Gaussian belief with a Gaussian measurement gives a Gaussian, with the inverse-variance weighting from the measurement-noise lesson. This is its update step.

Worked example

A robot believes its position along a hallway is $\mathcal{N}(0, 4)$: mean 0 m, variance 4 ($\sigma = 2$ m). A sensor reads 3 m with variance 1. Weighting each by the inverse of its variance:

$$\mu_{\text{post}} = \frac{0/4 + 3/1}{1/4 + 1} = \frac{3}{1.25} = 2.4\ \text{m}, \qquad \sigma^2_{\text{post}} = \frac{1}{1.25} = 0.8$$

The estimate moves most of the way toward the more trustworthy sensor, and the uncertainty ends up smaller than either one alone.

For the linear-map rule: if $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1)$ and $A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 1)$, the new covariance is $A\Sigma A^\top = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1)$, because stretching by 2 multiplies the variance by $2^2$.

Common mistake: mixing up standard deviation and variance. Variances add and scale by the square; standard deviations don't. Doubling a quantity doubles $\sigma$ but quadruples $\sigma^2$.

V.t: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs
A pretty reason why Gaussian + Gaussian = Gaussian

odes.s: Derivatives, Jacobians, and ordinary differential equations, used to describe how state changes over time.
i: An ODE $\dot x = f(x, u)$ specifies how the state changes at each instant; given an initial condition and input history, it determines the whole future trajectory (under mild smoothness conditions).

The Jacobian $\partial f/\partial x$ is the matrix of partial derivatives; it gives the best linear approximation $f(x + \delta x) \approx f(x) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\delta x$ near a point.
Equilibria satisfy $f(x^*, u^*) = 0$; for the scalar ODE $\dot x = a x$ the solution is $x(t) = e^{a t} x(0)$, which decays if $a < 0$ and grows if $a > 0$.
q: For $\dot x = -2x + u$ with $u = 0$ and $x(0) = 3$, what happens to $x(t)$?
It grows exponentially as $3e^{2t}$
It oscillates around 0 with period $\pi$
It decays exponentially to 0 as $3e^{-2t}$
It decreases linearly and reaches 0 at $t = 1.5$
The solution of $\dot x = a x$ is $x(0)e^{a t}$; with $a = -2$ it decays exponentially. Linear decrease would require a constant rate, not one proportional to x.
odes.t: Compute the Jacobian of $f(x) = (x_2,\ -\sin x_1)$ (a pendulum) by hand, then check it at $x = (0, 0)$ against finite differences in NumPy.
odes.T:
What an ODE says

A derivative is a rate of change: $\dot x = \frac{dx}{dt}$ is how fast $x$ moves right now. An ordinary differential equation says how that rate depends on where you are and what you do:

$$\dot x = f(x, u)$$

Every model in this course has this shape. A robot rolling forward, a drone climbing, a car turning: each is a rule for the rate of change of its state $x$ given its input $u$.

Solving one means rolling time forward

The ODE doesn't hand you $x(t)$ directly. You get it by adding up all the small changes, which is integration. A few simple ODEs have exact answers. The most important one:

$$\dot x = -a\,x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(t) = x_0\, e^{-a t}$$

For $a > 0$ it decays to zero, faster for bigger $a$. For $a < 0$ it grows without bound. You'll see this decay shape again every time a controller pulls an error to zero.

When there's no formula: step it

Most robot models have no closed-form solution, so we step them on a computer. The simplest method, forward Euler, assumes the rate stays fixed for a short time $h$:

$$x_{k+1} = x_k + h\, f(x_k, u_k)$$

Smaller $h$ is more accurate but takes more steps. Better methods (Runge-Kutta) take a few looks at $f$ inside each step.

Higher derivatives become more state

Newton's law for a cart, $m\,\ddot q = u$, has a second derivative. Stack position and velocity into one vector, $x = (q, \dot q)$, and it becomes first-order: $\dot x = (\dot q,\ u/m)$. This trick is how every mechanical system gets into the form $\dot x = f(x, u)$, and it's the next lesson.

Worked example

Step $\dot x = -2x$ from $x_0 = 1$ with Euler, $h = 0.1$: each step multiplies by $1 + h(-2) = 0.8$, so $x_1 = 0.8$ and $x_2 = 0.64$. The exact answer is $e^{-0.4} \approx 0.670$ at $t = 0.2$, so Euler is a little low after two steps. Halve $h$ to $0.05$ and the four-step answer, $0.9^4 \approx 0.656$, is closer.

Common mistake: picking $h$ too big. Here, $h = 1.5$ gives a multiplier of $1 - 3 = -2$, so the simulation flips sign and explodes even though the true system decays.

V.t: Differential equations, a tourist's guide

optimization.s: Minimizing a cost subject to constraints: gradients, optimality conditions, and the solvers that trajectory optimization and calibration run on.
i: For unconstrained smooth problems, a local minimum has zero gradient and positive semidefinite Hessian; gradient descent steps along -∇f, while Newton's method uses the Hessian for faster local convergence.
With constraints, the KKT conditions generalize ∇f = 0: at an optimum the cost gradient is a combination of active constraint gradients, weighted by Lagrange multipliers.
Convex problems (convex cost, convex feasible set) have every local minimum global; nonconvex ones, like most trajectory optimization, depend on initialization.
q: A nonlinear trajectory optimizer returns different solutions when started from two different initial guesses. What is the most likely explanation?
The solver has a bug, since optimizers must return a unique answer
The constraints are linear, which always produces multiple optima
The step size was too small for the solver to reach the minimum
The problem is nonconvex, so the solver converges to different local minima
Nonconvex problems can have many local minima, and local solvers find the one near the initial guess. Linear constraints with a convex cost would give a unique global optimum value.
optimization.t: Minimize f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + x with gradient descent starting from x = -2 and x = 2, and note which local minimum each run finds.

L.title: Course Overview and Intro to Nonlinear Optimization

optimization.T:
What an optimizer is looking for

An optimization problem asks for the $x$ that makes a cost $f(x)$ as small as possible. Without constraints, a smooth local minimum has two signatures:

  • the gradient is zero, $\nabla f(x^*) = 0$, so no direction goes downhill to first order
  • the Hessian $\nabla^2 f(x^*)$ is positive semidefinite, so the surface curves up, not down.

A zero gradient alone isn't enough: maxima and saddle points have it too. Trajectory optimization, calibration and SLAM all come down to this search, just with many more variables.

Two ways to walk downhill

Gradient descent steps against the slope with a step size $\alpha$:

$$x_{k+1} = x_k - \alpha\, \nabla f(x_k)$$

It is cheap per step but slow in long, narrow valleys. Newton's method also uses curvature, jumping to the minimum of the local quadratic model:

$$x_{k+1} = x_k - \left[\nabla^2 f(x_k)\right]^{-1} \nabla f(x_k)$$

Near a minimum it converges much faster, but each step needs the Hessian and a linear solve, and far from a minimum it can head the wrong way. Practical solvers blend the two.

Constraints and the KKT conditions

Most robot problems have constraints: minimize $f(x)$ subject to $h(x) = 0$ and $g(x) \le 0$. At a constrained optimum you can't go downhill without leaving the feasible set, so the cost gradient must be balanced by the constraint gradients:

$$\nabla f + \textstyle\sum_i \lambda_i \nabla h_i + \sum_j \mu_j \nabla g_j = 0$$

These are the KKT conditions, together with $\mu_j \ge 0$ and $\mu_j\, g_j(x) = 0$. The last one says an inequality only pushes back when it is active ($g_j = 0$). The weights $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are the Lagrange multipliers.

Worked example: closest point on a line

Minimize $f = x^2 + y^2$ subject to $h = x + y - 1 = 0$. The gradients are $\nabla f = (2x, 2y)$ and $\nabla h = (1, 1)$, so KKT gives

$$2x + \lambda = 0, \qquad 2y + \lambda = 0, \qquad x + y = 1$$

The first two force $x = y$, the third gives $x = y = 0.5$, and then $\lambda = -1$. The cost is $0.5$. Geometrically, the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 0.5$ just touches the line there, so the two gradients are parallel.

Convex problems are the easy ones

A problem is convex when the cost is convex and the feasible set is convex. Then every local minimum is a global minimum, and solvers come with guarantees. Least squares, LQR and many MPC problems are convex.

Most trajectory optimization isn't: nonlinear dynamics and obstacles bend the feasible set. Then the solver returns the local minimum nearest its starting guess, and two guesses can give two different answers.

Common mistake: blaming the solver when a nonconvex problem gives different answers from different starts. That's expected. Give it a good initial guess, such as a straight-line path or the previous solution.

V.t: Gradient Descent in 3 minutes
The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) Conditions and the Interior Point Method for Convex Optimization

deep_learning_basics.s: Layers, losses, backpropagation, and stochastic gradient descent. Needed for learned perception and learned policies.
i: A neural network composes layers h = σ(W x + b); the nonlinearity σ (ReLU, tanh) is what lets stacks of layers represent functions beyond a single linear map.

Training minimizes a loss (e.g. mean squared error or cross-entropy) over parameters; backpropagation is the chain rule applied efficiently to get the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight.
Stochastic gradient descent updates weights using gradients from small minibatches; it is cheaper per step than full-batch descent and the noise is tolerated or even helpful.
q: You remove every nonlinearity from a 5-layer network. What can the resulting network represent?
Only affine functions, since a composition of linear layers is itself linear
Any continuous function, since depth alone gives universal approximation
Only constant functions, because gradients vanish without activations
Polynomials up to degree 5, one degree contributed per layer
W5(...(W1 x + b1)...) + b5 collapses to a single W x + b. Depth without nonlinearity adds no expressive power, so it cannot approximate arbitrary functions.
deep_learning_basics.t: In NumPy, fit y = sin(x) on [-3, 3] with a one-hidden-layer ReLU network trained by hand-coded backprop and SGD, and plot the fit after 2000 steps.
deep_learning_basics.T:
A network is a stack of simple layers

A neural network is a function built from layers. Each layer multiplies its input by a weight matrix, adds a bias, and applies a simple nonlinearity $\sigma$:

$$h = \sigma(W x + b)$$

A common choice is the ReLU, $\sigma(z) = \max(0, z)$. The nonlinearity is essential: without it, stacked layers multiply out to a single matrix, and the network could only represent linear maps. With it, enough layers can approximate almost any function, such as from pixels to "is there a pedestrian here?"

The loss says what "good" means

Training needs a single number to minimize, the loss, averaged over examples.

  • For predicting numbers (regression), mean squared error: $L = \tfrac{1}{N} \sum_i (\hat y_i - y_i)^2$.
  • For choosing among classes, the network outputs probabilities through a softmax, and cross-entropy penalizes a low probability on the correct class: $L = -\log p_{\text{correct}}$. Predicting the right class with $p = 0.9$ costs $0.11$; with $p = 0.1$ it costs $2.3$.

Backpropagation is the chain rule

To improve the weights you need $\partial L / \partial w$ for every weight, often millions of them. Backpropagation gets all of them in one backward sweep. The forward pass computes and stores each layer's output. Then, starting from the loss, the chain rule passes derivatives back layer by layer, each layer reusing the result from the layer after it. The cost is about twice a forward pass, whatever the number of weights. Frameworks such as PyTorch do this automatically.

Stochastic gradient descent

Training repeats one simple update:

$$\theta \leftarrow \theta - \alpha\, \nabla_\theta L_{\text{batch}}$$

Here the gradient is computed on a small random minibatch, say 32 examples, rather than the full dataset. Each step is cheap and noisy, and the noise even helps escape poor regions. The learning rate $\alpha$ is the most important setting: too large and training diverges, too small and it crawls. Popular variants such as Adam adapt the step for each weight.

Worked example: one gradient step

A single weight predicts $\hat y = w x$. Take input $x = 2$, target $y = 3$, current $w = 1$, and loss $L = \tfrac12 (\hat y - y)^2$.

  • Forward: $\hat y = 2$, so $L = \tfrac12 (2 - 3)^2 = 0.5$.
  • Backward: $\partial L / \partial w = (\hat y - y)\, x = (-1)(2) = -2$.
  • Update with $\alpha = 0.1$: $w = 1 - 0.1 \times (-2) = 1.2$.

Now $\hat y = 2.4$ and $L = 0.18$. Repeating drives $w$ toward $1.5$.

Common mistake: judging a model by its training loss. A big network can memorize its training set. Trust the loss on held-out validation data instead.

V.t: But what is a neural network? | Deep learning chapter 1
Backpropagation, intuitively | Deep Learning Chapter 3

autonomy_software.s: The Python tooling and the idea of a modular stack where perception, estimation, planning, and control run as connected components.
i: An autonomy stack splits the robot's job into modules: perception turns raw sensor data into features or objects, estimation tracks the robot's state, planning picks a path, and control turns it into actuator commands.
Modules communicate through well-defined messages (e.g. publish/subscribe topics as in ROS), so each can be developed, tested, and replaced independently.
Modules run at different rates: a low-level controller may run at hundreds of Hz while a global planner replans only occasionally, so interfaces must tolerate stale or asynchronous data.
q: Your planner runs at 1 Hz but the controller runs at 100 Hz. What should the controller do between planner updates?
Stop and wait for the next plan so it never acts on stale information
Keep tracking the most recent plan using fresh state estimates each cycle
Re-run the planner itself every cycle to match its own update rate
Repeat the last actuator command unchanged until a new plan arrives
Fast feedback on the latest plan is the point of a layered stack; the controller corrects disturbances using current state. Holding the last command open-loop discards that feedback.
autonomy_software.t: Sketch a block diagram for a robot that drives to a goal: list each module, the message it publishes, the topics it subscribes to, and a plausible update rate.

state_space.s: Describe a robot by a state vector and inputs, with dynamics giving the state's rate of change. Every later control and estimation method starts here.
i: The state $x$ is the smallest set of variables that, together with future inputs $u$, determines the future evolution; dynamics are written $\dot x = f(x, u)$ or $x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k)$.
A higher-order ODE becomes first-order state-space form by stacking derivatives: $m\ddot q = u$ becomes $x = (q, \dot q)$ with $\dot x = (\dot q,\ u/m)$.
Linear time-invariant models $\dot x = Ax + Bu$, $y = Cx$ are the special case where controllability, stability, and estimation have clean matrix tests.
q: For a mass on a frictionless track pushed by force $u$, why is position alone not a valid state?
Because force must always be included in the state vector
Because position is not measurable, so it cannot be a state
Because the future depends on velocity too, which position alone does not fix
Because state vectors must have at least three components
Knowing position and the future force does not determine motion unless velocity is known, so the state is $(q, \dot q)$. Inputs like force are not part of the state.
state_space.t: Write the pendulum $m l^2 \ddot\theta = -m g l \sin\theta + u$ in the form $\dot x = f(x, u)$ with $x = (\theta, \dot\theta)$.

L.title: Course Overview and Mobile Robot Kinematics

state_space.T:
What "state" means

The state $x$ is the smallest set of numbers that, together with the inputs you'll apply from now on, fixes everything that happens next. If two identical robots have the same state and get the same inputs, they do exactly the same thing. A state-space model writes the rule for how state changes:

$$\dot x = f(x, u), \qquad y = h(x)$$

Here $u$ is the input you control (forces, wheel speeds) and $y$ is what your sensors measure. The output and the state are often different: you might measure only position while the state also includes velocity.

Finding the state of a mechanical system

Newton's law gives second derivatives, so position alone is never enough. For a cart of mass $m$ pushed by force $u$, $m\,\ddot q = u$. Knowing where the cart is doesn't tell you where it will be: you also need how fast it's moving. So the state is $x = (q, \dot q)$, and

$$\dot x = \begin{bmatrix} \dot q \\ u/m \end{bmatrix}$$

The linear special case

When $f$ is linear, the model becomes matrices:

$$\dot x = A x + B u, \qquad y = C x$$

For the cart: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, $B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1/m \end{bmatrix}$, and $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ if you measure position. Linear models matter because questions like "is it stable?", "can I steer it anywhere?" and "can I estimate the state from $y$?" become linear-algebra tests on $A$, $B$ and $C$.

In discrete time

Computers act in steps, so you'll also see $x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k)$. With Euler steps of length $h$, the cart becomes $q_{k+1} = q_k + h\,\dot q_k$ and $\dot q_{k+1} = \dot q_k + h\,u_k/m$.

Worked example

A pendulum of length $l$ and mass $m$ with torque $u$ obeys $m l^2\, \ddot\theta = -m g l \sin\theta + u$. Take $x = (\theta, \dot\theta)$:

$$\dot x = \begin{bmatrix} \dot\theta \\ -\dfrac{g}{l}\sin\theta + \dfrac{u}{m l^2} \end{bmatrix}$$

That's nonlinear because of $\sin\theta$. Lesson 7 shows how to approximate it with $A$ and $B$ near a point.

Common mistake: putting the input in the state. Force $u$ is something you choose at each moment, so it's not part of $x$.

V.t: Introduction to State-Space Equations

kinematic_models.s: Kinematic models relate velocities to motion and ignore forces; dynamic models include mass, inertia, and actuation. Choosing the right fidelity is a design decision.
i: A kinematic model treats velocities (or wheel speeds) as the inputs and integrates them to get pose; it ignores mass, inertia, and forces.
A dynamic model takes forces or torques as inputs and includes mass and inertia, so velocities become states that cannot change instantly.
Kinematic models suffice at low speeds and accelerations where actuators track commanded velocities well; at high speed, tire slip and inertia make dynamic models necessary.
q: A planner built on a kinematic car model commands a sharp speed change, and the real car lags behind. What does the model miss?
The nonholonomic constraint that prevents sideways sliding
The heading angle, which kinematic models do not track
The position integration that converts velocity to pose
Inertia and actuator limits, which stop velocity from changing instantly

Kinematic models treat velocity as directly commanded, so they assume instant speed changes; the lag comes from mass and limited force. Kinematic car models still include heading and the no-slip constraint.
kinematic_models.t: Simulate a 1D cart both as $\dot x = v$ (kinematic) and as $\ddot x = (u - b\dot x)/m$ (dynamic) for a step command, and plot how the dynamic one lags.

L.title: Course Overview and Mobile Robot Kinematics

kinematic_models.T:
Two levels of detail

A kinematic model treats velocities as the inputs. It captures the geometry of how a robot can move and ignores what it takes to get those velocities: mass, inertia and forces. A dynamic model treats forces or torques as the inputs, so velocities become part of the state and can't change instantly.

The unicycle: the kinematic workhorse

A wheeled robot that drives forward at speed $v$ and turns at rate $\omega$, with pose $(x, y, \theta)$:

$$\dot x = v\cos\theta, \qquad \dot y = v\sin\theta, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega$$

Notice what's missing: there's no way to move sideways. The wheels roll but don't slide. That's the robot's geometry, and the kinematic model gets it exactly right with only three states.

Adding dynamics

Real motors can't change speed instantly. The book's dynamically extended unicycle makes speed a state and acceleration the input:

$$\dot x = v\cos\theta, \quad \dot y = v\sin\theta, \quad \dot v = a, \quad \dot\theta = \omega$$

with state $(x, y, v, \theta)$ and inputs $(a, \omega)$. Going further, a full dynamic model adds mass, tire forces and motor torques.

Which to use

Use the kinematic model when the robot is slow and its motors track the speeds you command well: indoor robots, warehouse carts, path planning. Use a dynamic model when forces matter: high speed, hard braking, tire slip, heavy loads. The trade-off is fidelity against simplicity, and choosing it is a design decision.

Worked example

Drive the unicycle with constant $v = 1\ \text{m/s}$ and $\omega = 0.5\ \text{rad/s}$. The heading grows at a constant rate while the speed stays fixed, so the robot drives a circle of radius

$$r = \frac{v}{\omega} = \frac{1}{0.5} = 2\ \text{m}$$

and comes back around after $2\pi/\omega \approx 12.6$ s. In the dynamically extended model, you'd first have to accelerate from rest: with $a = 0.5\ \text{m/s}^2$, it takes 2 s to reach $v = 1$.

Common mistake: trusting a kinematic plan at high speed. The kinematic model will happily command an instant change of speed that the real robot can't follow.

V.t: Kinematic bicycle model
V.ch: Prof. Georg Schildbach, University of Lübeck

nonholonomic.s: Wheels that cannot slide sideways constrain velocity but not position. The unicycle and differential-drive models capture this and recur through the book.
i: The unicycle model $\dot x = v\cos\theta$, $\dot y = v\sin\theta$, $\dot\theta = \omega$ captures a robot that can drive forward and turn but cannot move sideways.
The no-slip condition $\dot x\sin\theta - \dot y\cos\theta = 0$ restricts velocity, but it cannot be integrated into a constraint on position, so every pose is still reachable.
A differential-drive robot maps to the unicycle via $v = r(\omega_R + \omega_L)/2$ and $\omega = r(\omega_R - \omega_L)/L$, with wheel radius $r$ and axle length $L$.
q: A unicycle robot needs to move 1 m sideways (perpendicular to its heading). Is that possible?
Yes, by a maneuver such as turning, driving, and turning back, like parallel parking
No, because the nonholonomic constraint forbids any change in lateral position
Yes, but only if the wheels are allowed to slip temporarily
No, unless it has three or more independently driven wheels
The constraint limits instantaneous velocity, not reachable positions, so a sequence of feasible motions achieves the shift. Forbidding lateral position change would be a holonomic constraint.
nonholonomic.t: Integrate the unicycle with Euler steps for $v = 1$, $\omega = 0.5$ for 4 seconds starting at the origin, and check that the path is an arc of radius $v/\omega = 2$.

nonholonomic.T:
Wheels that can't slide

A car or a wheeled robot can drive forward and turn, but it can't slide straight sideways: the wheels grip the floor. That's a limit on how the robot can move right now, a constraint on its velocity. For the unicycle with pose $(x, y, \theta)$, "no sideways motion" says the velocity has no component perpendicular to the heading:

$$\dot x \sin\theta - \dot y \cos\theta = 0$$

Why it's called nonholonomic

Some constraints limit where you can be: a bead on a wire can never leave the wire. Those are holonomic. The no-slip rule is different. It limits velocity, but it can't be rewritten as a rule about position, so every pose is still reachable. That's what nonholonomic means. You've done this every time you parallel park: you can't slide into the space, but a sequence of allowed motions (back, turn, forward) gets the car there.

The unicycle and the differential drive

The kinematic model that respects the constraint is the unicycle from lesson 2:

$$\dot x = v\cos\theta, \qquad \dot y = v\sin\theta, \qquad \dot\theta = \omega$$

Most indoor robots are differential drive: two wheels of radius $r$ on an axle of length $L$, each with its own motor. Their wheel speeds $\omega_R$ and $\omega_L$ map onto the unicycle's inputs:

$$v = \frac{r(\omega_R + \omega_L)}{2}, \qquad \omega = \frac{r(\omega_R - \omega_L)}{L}$$

Equal wheel speeds drive straight; opposite speeds spin in place.

Worked example

A robot with $r = 0.05$ m and $L = 0.3$ m spins its wheels at $\omega_R = 12$ and $\omega_L = 8$ rad/s. Then

$$v = \frac{0.05 \times 20}{2} = 0.5\ \text{m/s}, \qquad \omega = \frac{0.05 \times 4}{0.3} \approx 0.67\ \text{rad/s}$$

so it drives a circle of radius $v/\omega = 0.75$ m. To drive straight at the same speed, set both wheels to 10 rad/s.

Common mistake: concluding that a nonholonomic robot can't reach a sideways position. It can; it just can't get there in one straight move. Planners have to respect that, which is why parking takes maneuvers.

simulation.s: Step continuous dynamics forward in time with Euler or Runge–Kutta schemes, and understand when discretization error matters.
i: Forward Euler x_{k+1} = x_k + h f(x_k, u_k) is simple but first-order: its global error scales with step size h.
Runge-Kutta 4 combines four slope evaluations per step and has global error of order h^4, so it is far more accurate for the same step size.
Explicit methods can go unstable on fast or oscillatory dynamics: Euler on x_dot = -a x is stable only when h < 2/a, and on an undamped oscillator it spirals outward, adding energy.
q: You simulate an undamped spring-mass system with forward Euler and the amplitude slowly grows. What is happening?
The spring constant was entered with the wrong sign, adding energy
Euler's discretization error injects energy each step for oscillatory dynamics
Floating-point rounding accumulates, and this would vanish in double precision
The system is physically unstable and RK4 would show the same growth

Forward Euler multiplies the oscillator state by a matrix with eigenvalue magnitude sqrt(1 + (hω)^2) > 1, so amplitude grows. The real system conserves energy, and RK4 would stay much closer to constant.
simulation.t: Simulate x_ddot = -x for 20 s with h = 0.1 using Euler and RK4, and plot the energy (x^2 + x_dot^2)/2 for both.

optimal_control.s: Pose motion as choosing inputs that minimize a cost while respecting dynamics and constraints, producing an open-loop plan.
i: An optimal control problem chooses u(t) to minimize J = h(x(t_f)) + ∫ g(x, u) dt subject to x_dot = f(x, u), initial conditions, and state and input constraints.
The cost encodes design trade-offs: penalizing u^2 trades effort for speed, terminal costs pull toward goals, and changing weights changes which trajectory is 'optimal'.
The solution is an open-loop input sequence; it is optimal only for the model and initial state assumed, so disturbances require feedback or replanning.
q: You solve an optimal control problem offline and play the resulting inputs on a real robot. A gust pushes it off course early on. What happens?
The inputs automatically adjust because the solution was optimal
The robot returns to the plan since the cost function penalizes deviation
The open-loop inputs do not react, so the error persists or grows
The robot stops because the dynamics constraint is no longer satisfied
An open-loop plan is a fixed input sequence with no measurement of the actual state, so it cannot correct a disturbance. The cost only shaped the plan offline; it does not act at run time.
optimal_control.t: For a double integrator, write out the cost, dynamics, and boundary conditions for moving from rest at 0 to rest at 1 in 2 s while minimizing ∫ u^2 dt.
optimal_control.T:
The problem in one line

Optimal control picks the input signal $u(t)$ that makes a cost as small as possible while obeying the dynamics:

$$\min_{u(\cdot)}\; J = h\big(x(t_f)\big) + \int_0^{t_f} g\big(x(t), u(t)\big)\, dt$$

subject to $\dot x = f(x, u)$, a known start $x(0) = x_0$, and limits on states and inputs. Here $h$ is a terminal cost (how far from the goal you end up) and $g$ is a running cost (effort, time, discomfort). The answer is a whole trajectory, not a single number.

The cost is where you make design choices

The "optimal" trajectory is only optimal for the cost you wrote. Some common terms:

  • $g = 1$ gives minimum time.
  • $g = u^\top R\, u$ penalizes effort, giving smoother, gentler motion.
  • $h = (x - x_g)^\top Q_f (x - x_g)$ pulls the final state toward a goal $x_g$.

Changing the weights changes the answer. A large $R$ gives a slow, efficient move; a small $R$ gives a fast, aggressive one. Choosing weights is engineering judgment, not something the math decides for you.

Worked example: moving a cart in one second

A cart with $\ddot q = u$ starts at rest at $q = 0$ and must stop at rest at $q = 1$ at $t_f = 1$ s, minimizing effort $\int_0^1 u^2\, dt$. The optimal input turns out to be a straight line in time:

$$u(t) = 6 - 12t, \qquad q(t) = 3t^2 - 2t^3$$

Check: $q(1) = 3 - 2 = 1$, $\dot q = 6t - 6t^2$ is zero at both ends, and $\ddot q = 6 - 12t = u$. The cart pushes hard at first, coasts through the middle, and brakes at the end. The total cost is $\int_0^1 (6 - 12t)^2\, dt = 12$.

An open-loop plan only fits the model you assumed

The solution is a schedule of inputs, computed once from $x_0$. If the real cart is heavier than modeled, or someone bumps it, the schedule keeps playing anyway and the cart misses the goal.

So in practice an optimal trajectory is paired with feedback: a tracking controller (PID, LQR) that corrects deviations from the plan, or model predictive control, which re-solves the problem from the measured state every few milliseconds.

Common mistake: expecting an optimal open-loop trajectory to be robust. It is the best plan for a perfect model, and often the most fragile, because it uses every margin the model allows.

Two ways to solve it

  • Indirect methods first derive optimality conditions (Pontryagin's principle), then solve those equations numerically.
  • Direct methods first chop the trajectory into time steps, then hand the resulting finite problem to a numerical optimizer.

Indirect methods can be very accurate; direct methods handle constraints easily and are what most robotics software uses. The next two lessons cover each.

indirect_methods.s: Derive necessary conditions for optimality first, then solve them. This turns trajectory optimization into a boundary value problem.
i: Pontryagin's principle introduces costates p and the Hamiltonian H = g(x, u) + p^T f(x, u); the optimal input minimizes H at each time.
Necessary conditions are x_dot = ∂H/∂p, p_dot = -∂H/∂x, plus boundary conditions on x(0) and on x(t_f) or p(t_f), giving a two-point boundary value problem.
Indirect methods can be very accurate but are sensitive: shooting on the costate initial value often diverges without a good guess, and inequality constraints complicate the conditions.
q: Why does solving Pontryagin's conditions usually lead to a two-point boundary value problem rather than a simple forward simulation?
Because the Hamiltonian must be minimized at both endpoints separately
Because the costate equations are only defined at the final time
Because the dynamics must be integrated backward in time to stay stable
Because x is fixed at t = 0 while p is constrained at t_f, so neither is fully known at one end

The state's initial value and the costate's terminal condition sit at opposite ends, so you cannot integrate forward from a fully known start. Costates are defined over the whole interval, not only at t_f.
indirect_methods.t: For x_dot = u minimizing ∫ u^2/2 dt from x(0)=0 to x(1)=1, form H, derive p_dot = 0 and u = -p, and solve for the constant optimal u.

L.title: Pontryagin's Minimum Principle and Computational Methods

indirect_methods.T:
Optimality conditions first, numbers second

An indirect method doesn't search over trajectories directly. It first asks what any optimal trajectory must satisfy, then solves those conditions. The tool is Pontryagin's principle. Attach a costate $p(t)$, one entry per state, and form the Hamiltonian:

$$H(x, u, p) = g(x, u) + p^\top f(x, u)$$

The costate plays the role a Lagrange multiplier plays in ordinary optimization: it measures how much the cost would change if the state at time $t$ were nudged.

The necessary conditions

Along an optimal trajectory:

$$\dot x = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p} = f(x, u), \qquad \dot p = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}, \qquad u^* = \arg\min_u H$$

When $u$ is unconstrained, the last condition becomes $\partial H / \partial u = 0$. Add the boundary conditions: $x(0) = x_0$ is fixed, and at the end either $x(t_f)$ is given, or it is free and $p(t_f) = \partial h / \partial x$ at $x(t_f)$.

Worked example: the cart again

Take $\ddot q = u$ with state $(q, v)$, cost $\int_0^1 \tfrac12 u^2\, dt$, from rest at $0$ to rest at $1$. Then

$$H = \tfrac12 u^2 + p_1 v + p_2 u$$
  • $\partial H/\partial u = u + p_2 = 0$, so $u = -p_2$.
  • $\dot p_1 = -\partial H/\partial q = 0$, so $p_1 = c_1$ is constant.
  • $\dot p_2 = -\partial H/\partial v = -p_1$, so $p_2 = c_2 - c_1 t$.

So the optimal input is linear in time, $u = c_1 t - c_2$. The four boundary conditions fix the two constants: $c_1 = -12$, $c_2 = -6$, giving $u = 6 - 12t$.

A two-point boundary value problem

The example could be solved by hand; most can't. The trouble is that the conditions are split: $x$ is known at $t = 0$, but $p$ is only pinned down at $t_f$. You can't just integrate forward.

Shooting guesses the missing $p(0)$, integrates $x$ and $p$ forward together, measures how badly the end conditions are missed, and corrects the guess with a root finder. Because the costate equations are often unstable forward in time, small errors in the guess can blow up.

Accurate, but touchy

When indirect methods converge they are very accurate, since they solve exact optimality conditions. The price:

  • They need a good initial guess for the costate, which has no obvious physical meaning.
  • Inequality constraints (torque limits, obstacles) split the trajectory into arcs where different conditions apply, and you must know the arc structure in advance.

That is why robotics software mostly uses direct methods, and keeps indirect ones for problems with clean structure, such as orbit transfers.

Common mistake: treating any solution of these conditions as the optimum. Pontryagin's conditions are necessary, not sufficient: a trajectory can satisfy them and still be a local optimum, or not a minimum at all.

V.t: L7.1 Pontryagin's principle of maximum (minimum) and its application to optimal control

direct_methods.s: Discretize the trajectory and hand the whole problem to a nonlinear solver. The workhorse of practical trajectory optimization.
i: Direct methods discretize first: choose decision variables such as x_0..x_N and u_0..u_{N-1}, then optimize with a nonlinear programming solver.
In direct collocation or multiple shooting, dynamics become equality constraints like x_{k+1} = x_k + h f(x_k, u_k), so infeasible guesses are allowed and the solver repairs them.
Path and input constraints (obstacles, torque limits) are added directly as inequalities, which is a main reason direct methods dominate in practice.
q: In direct transcription with both states and inputs as decision variables, why can you initialize with a straight-line state guess that violates the dynamics?
Because dynamics are enforced as constraints the solver satisfies at convergence
Because the solver ignores dynamics and only optimizes the cost function
Because a straight line is always dynamically feasible for wheeled robots
Because the initial guess is discarded before the first iteration begins
Defect constraints x_{k+1} - F(x_k, u_k) = 0 need only hold at the solution, so intermediate iterates may be infeasible. The dynamics are not ignored; they are constraints.
direct_methods.t: Use scipy.optimize.minimize (SLSQP) to move a double integrator from 0 to 1 in N = 20 steps, with x_k and u_k as variables and Euler dynamics as equality constraints.
direct_methods.T:
Discretize first, then optimize

A direct method turns the infinite-dimensional problem (a whole function $u(t)$) into a finite one. Split $[0, t_f]$ into $N$ steps of length $\Delta t$, and make the states and inputs at each step the unknowns:

$$z = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_N,\; u_0, \dots, u_{N-1})$$

The integral cost becomes a sum, $J \approx h(x_N) + \sum_k g(x_k, u_k)\, \Delta t$. Now it is an ordinary nonlinear program, and a general solver (IPOPT, SNOPT, or an SQP method) can take it from there.

The dynamics become equality constraints

The solver doesn't simulate. Instead, each step of the dynamics is a constraint that ties neighboring variables together. With Euler integration:

$$x_{k+1} = x_k + \Delta t\, f(x_k, u_k), \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1$$

This is the collocation (or multiple shooting) view. Its big practical advantage: the initial guess doesn't have to obey the dynamics. You can start from a straight line that cuts through obstacles, with zero inputs, and the solver repairs the violated constraints while it lowers the cost. Single shooting, which keeps only the inputs as unknowns and simulates, is smaller but much more sensitive to the guess.

Constraints go straight in

Anything you can write as an equation or inequality on $z$ becomes part of the problem:

  • input limits, $-u_{\max} \le u_k \le u_{\max}$
  • obstacles, $\|p_k - c\| \ge r$ for a round obstacle at $c$ with radius $r$
  • start and goal, $x_0 = x_{\text{start}}$, $x_N = x_{\text{goal}}$.

This ease with constraints is the main reason direct methods dominate practical trajectory optimization. Indirect methods need the constraint structure worked out by hand.

Worked example: counting the unknowns

Take the cart $\ddot q = u$ with state $(q, v)$, from rest at $0$ to rest at $1$.

With $N = 2$ and $\Delta t = 0.5$: there are $3 \times 2 = 6$ state variables and $2$ inputs, so $8$ unknowns. Constraints: $2$ (start) $+ 4$ (dynamics) $+ 2$ (goal), also $8$. So the answer is forced: Euler gives $q_2 = 0.25\,u_0 = 1$ and $v_2 = 0.5(u_0 + u_1) = 0$, so $u_0 = 4$, $u_1 = -4$. Nothing is left to optimize.

With $N = 10$: $22 + 10 = 32$ unknowns and $2 + 20 + 2 = 24$ constraints, leaving $8$ degrees of freedom for the cost to choose.

Why the solver stays fast

The problem looks big, but each dynamics constraint touches only $x_k$, $u_k$ and $x_{k+1}$. The constraint Jacobian is therefore mostly zeros, in a banded pattern, and solvers exploit that sparsity. Problems with thousands of variables solve in milliseconds to seconds.

Common mistake: trusting a plan built on a coarse grid. The solver satisfies the discretized dynamics exactly, so it happily exploits Euler's errors. Simulate the inputs with a fine, accurate integrator before you run them on a robot.

differential_flatness.s: For some systems, all states and inputs follow from a few flat outputs and their derivatives, so smooth trajectories can be designed in those outputs directly.
i: A system is differentially flat if there exist outputs $z$ (the flat outputs) such that every state and input can be written as a function of $z$ and finitely many of its derivatives.
For the unicycle, $z = (x, y)$ is flat: $v = \sqrt{\dot x^2 + \dot y^2}$, $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\dot y, \dot x)$, and $\omega$ follows from second derivatives, valid while $v \neq 0$.
Planning becomes curve fitting: choose smooth $z(t)$ (e.g. polynomials) meeting boundary conditions, and the dynamics are satisfied automatically.
q: Using flatness for a unicycle, you fit a polynomial path that stops partway with $\dot x = \dot y = 0$. What goes wrong at that instant?
Nothing, since flatness guarantees all states are defined everywhere
The heading $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\dot y, \dot x)$ becomes undefined, so the map breaks down
The position becomes discontinuous because the polynomial has zero slope
The robot must slide sideways to keep following the planned path
The flat map for the unicycle is singular at zero speed, where heading cannot be recovered from velocity. Position stays continuous; the problem is recovering $\theta$ and $\omega$.
differential_flatness.t: Pick $x(t) = t$, $y(t) = t^2$ for $t \in [0, 1]$ and compute the unicycle's $v(t)$, $\theta(t)$ and $\omega(t)$ from the flat outputs.
differential_flatness.T:
The problem it solves

Planning a trajectory usually means finding inputs $u(t)$ so that integrating $\dot x = f(x, u)$ lands where you want, and that's hard. For some systems there's a shortcut: pick a few outputs, plan those freely, and every state and input follows by algebra, with no integration at all.

The definition

A system is differentially flat if there are outputs $z$ (the flat outputs, as many as there are inputs) such that every state and every input can be written as a function of $z$ and a finite number of its derivatives:

$$x = \beta(z, \dot z, \ldots, z^{(q)}), \qquad u = \gamma(z, \dot z, \ldots, z^{(q)})$$

Cars, unicycles and quadrotors are all flat, which is why this idea is used so much in robotics.

The unicycle is flat in $(x, y)$

For the unicycle, the position $(x, y)$ is a flat output. If you know the path $x(t), y(t)$ and its derivatives, the heading is the direction of motion, the speed is how fast you move along it, and the turn rate is how fast the heading changes:

$$\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\dot y, \dot x), \qquad v = \sqrt{\dot x^2 + \dot y^2}, \qquad \omega = \frac{\dot x\,\ddot y - \dot y\,\ddot x}{\dot x^2 + \dot y^2}$$

So planning reduces to drawing a smooth curve in the plane, for example a polynomial in $t$ whose coefficients you pick to match the start and end positions and velocities.

Worked example

Plan $x(t) = t$, $y(t) = t^2$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. Then $\dot x = 1$, $\dot y = 2t$, $\ddot x = 0$, $\ddot y = 2$, so

$$v(t) = \sqrt{1 + 4t^2}, \qquad \theta(t) = \operatorname{atan2}(2t, 1), \qquad \omega(t) = \frac{2}{1 + 4t^2}$$

At the start, $v = 1$, $\theta = 0$ and $\omega = 2$. At the end, $v = \sqrt 5 \approx 2.24$ and the robot is turning more gently, $\omega = 0.4$. Those $v(t)$ and $\omega(t)$ are the open-loop inputs that drive the robot along the parabola.

Common mistake: planning a curve where the robot stops. At $v = 0$ the heading formula is undefined (the denominator $\dot x^2 + \dot y^2$ is zero), so keep the planned speed above zero, or treat stops as special cases.

V.t: Differential Flatness

pid.s: Feedback from the error, its integral, and its derivative. Simple, ubiquitous, and the baseline every other controller is compared against.
i: PID control sets $u = K_p e + K_i \int e\,dt + K_d\,\dot e$, where $e$ is the tracking error; each term handles present, past, and predicted error.
The integral term removes steady-state error from constant disturbances, but with actuator saturation it can wind up and cause overshoot, so anti-windup is used.
The derivative term adds damping but amplifies sensor noise, so it is usually filtered or computed on the measurement rather than the error.
q: A P-only controller holds a drone near but always slightly below its target altitude because gravity is not fully compensated. Which change fixes this steady offset?
Increasing $K_d$ to add more damping
Reducing $K_p$ so the controller is less aggressive
Adding an integral term so accumulated error builds up thrust
Filtering the altitude measurement more heavily
A constant disturbance needs a nonzero steady input at zero error, which only integral action provides. Derivative gain affects transients, not steady-state offset.
pid.t: Simulate $\dot x = u - 1$ (constant disturbance) with P control $u = 2(1 - x)$ and then with PI, and compare the final value of $x$.
pid.T:
Feedback in one line

Measure the error between where you want to be and where you are, $e(t) = r(t) - y(t)$, and push in proportion to it. A PID controller adds two more terms:

$$u(t) = K_p\, e(t) + K_i \int_0^t e(\tau)\, d\tau + K_d\, \dot e(t)$$

What each term does

  • Proportional ($K_p$) reacts to the error now. Bigger $K_p$ is faster but overshoots more.
  • Integral ($K_i$) adds up past error. It keeps pushing until the error is exactly zero, which is the only way to cancel a constant disturbance such as gravity, friction or a slope.
  • Derivative ($K_d$) reacts to how fast the error changes. It acts like damping and stops overshoot, but it amplifies sensor noise, so it's usually filtered.

Why the integral term is needed

Take a cart $m\,\ddot q = u + d$ with a constant push $d$ (a slope, say) and PD control. When everything settles, $\dot q = \ddot q = 0$, so $K_p e + d = 0$: the cart sits at a steady error $e = -d/K_p$. Raising $K_p$ shrinks the offset but never removes it. Add $K_i$ and the integral keeps growing until it supplies $-d$ by itself, at zero error.

Worked example: tuning by matching a second-order system

With PD on the cart and no disturbance, the closed loop is

$$\ddot q + \frac{K_d}{m}\,\dot q + \frac{K_p}{m}\,q = \frac{K_p}{m}\,r$$

That's a standard second-order system with natural frequency $\omega_n = \sqrt{K_p/m}$ and damping ratio $\zeta = \frac{K_d}{2\sqrt{m K_p}}$. For $m = 1$ kg, if you want $\omega_n = 2$ rad/s with no overshoot ($\zeta = 1$): $K_p = m\,\omega_n^2 = 4$ and $K_d = 2\zeta\sqrt{m K_p} = 4$.

Common mistake: integral windup. If the motor saturates, the integral keeps growing during the saturation and then overshoots badly. Real controllers clamp the integral (anti-windup).

V.t: What Is PID Control? | Understanding PID Control, Part 1

linearization.s: Approximate nonlinear dynamics near a point or trajectory with a linear model so linear tools apply. Automatic differentiation makes the Jacobians cheap.
i: Around an equilibrium $(x^*, u^*)$ with $f(x^*, u^*) = 0$, dynamics are approximated as $\dot{\delta x} \approx A\,\delta x + B\,\delta u$, with $A = \partial f/\partial x$ and $B = \partial f/\partial u$ evaluated there.
Linearizing about a trajectory instead of a point gives time-varying $A(t)$, $B(t)$, which is what trajectory tracking and iLQR use.

The approximation is only local: a controller designed on the linear model is guaranteed only near the linearization point, and automatic differentiation computes the Jacobians exactly to machine precision.
q: You linearize a pendulum about the downward equilibrium and design a controller that works well. Then you start it far from that point, nearly inverted. Why might it fail?
The Jacobians computed by autodiff are inaccurate at large angles
Linear models cannot represent any pendulum, even at small angles
The controller gains change sign automatically when the angle is large
The linear model is only accurate near the linearization point, so large deviations break its assumptions
$\sin\theta \approx \theta$ holds only for small deviations, so the design's guarantees are local. Autodiff Jacobians are exact; the issue is the linear model, not how it was computed.
linearization.t: Linearize the pendulum $\ddot\theta = -(g/l)\sin\theta + u$ about $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$, and compare the eigenvalues of $A$ in each case.
linearization.T:
The idea

Linear models have clean tools (eigenvalues, LQR, the Kalman filter); robots are nonlinear. Linearization replaces a nonlinear model with a linear one that's accurate near a chosen operating point, using the first-order Taylor expansion.

The recipe

Pick a nominal state and input $(\bar x, \bar u)$, or a whole nominal trajectory $(\bar x(t), \bar u(t))$. Write the true state as nominal plus a small deviation, $x = \bar x + \delta x$ and $u = \bar u + \delta u$. Expanding $f$ to first order gives deviation dynamics:

$$\dot{\delta x} \approx A\,\delta x + B\,\delta u, \qquad A = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\bigg|_{\bar x, \bar u}, \quad B = \frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\bigg|_{\bar x, \bar u}$$

$A$ and $B$ are Jacobians: matrices of partial derivatives. Along a trajectory they change with time, $A(t)$ and $B(t)$, but the model for the deviations is still linear.

Worked example: the unicycle driving straight

The unicycle with state $(x, y, \theta)$ and inputs $(v, \omega)$ has $f = (v\cos\theta,\ v\sin\theta,\ \omega)$. The Jacobians are

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & -v\sin\theta \\ 0 & 0 & v\cos\theta \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Linearize about driving straight along $x$ at $\bar v = 1$, $\bar\theta = 0$:

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Read off the physics: $\dot{\delta y} = \delta\theta$, so a small heading error makes the robot drift sideways at a rate equal to that error. And $\delta\omega$ steers $\delta\theta$. That's exactly the structure a lateral controller needs to correct drift.

Common mistake: trusting the linear model far from the operating point. At a heading error of $0.1$ rad, $\sin(0.1) \approx 0.0998$, which is fine. At $1$ rad, $\sin(1) \approx 0.84$, which is badly off. Re-linearize along the trajectory.

V.t: What Is Linearization?

lqr.s: For linear dynamics and quadratic cost, the optimal feedback is a fixed gain matrix from a Riccati equation. The default controller for stabilizing a robot near a setpoint.
i: LQR minimizes Σ (x_k^T Q x_k + u_k^T R u_k) subject to x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k; the optimal policy is linear state feedback u_k = -K x_k.
K comes from the Riccati equation, solved backward in time for finite horizons or as the algebraic Riccati equation for the infinite-horizon steady-state gain.
Q and R set the trade-off: larger Q penalizes state error and gives aggressive control, larger R penalizes effort and gives gentler control.
q: You increase R (the input weight) by a factor of 100 in an LQR design. What do you expect?
Smaller gains, gentler inputs, and slower convergence of the state
Larger gains and faster convergence, because inputs matter more
The same gain, because only the ratio of Q entries affects K
An unstable closed loop, because R must stay below Q

Penalizing effort more makes the optimal controller use less of it, so K shrinks and the state converges more slowly. K depends on Q relative to R, so scaling R alone does change it, and the closed loop stays stable under the usual stabilizability and detectability assumptions.
lqr.t: Use scipy.linalg.solve_discrete_are on a discretized double integrator, compute K = (R + B^T P B)^{-1} B^T P A, and see how K changes as R goes from 0.1 to 10.
lqr.T:
The problem LQR solves

LQR (linear quadratic regulator) is optimal control for the one case with a clean answer: linear dynamics and a quadratic cost.

$$x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k, \qquad J = \sum_{k} \left( x_k^\top Q\, x_k + u_k^\top R\, u_k \right)$$

$Q \succeq 0$ says how much you dislike being away from zero (the setpoint), and $R \succ 0$ how much you dislike using effort. For a robot, $x$ is usually the error from a setpoint, and $A$, $B$ come from linearizing the dynamics there.

The answer is a gain matrix

The optimal input is plain linear state feedback, $u_k = -K_k x_k$. The gains come from the Riccati recursion, run backward from the end of the horizon with $P_N = Q_f$:

$$K_k = (R + B^\top P_{k+1} B)^{-1} B^\top P_{k+1} A, \qquad P_k = Q + A^\top P_{k+1} (A - B K_k)$$

$x^\top P_k x$ is the optimal cost-to-go from state $x$ at step $k$. Run the recursion long enough and $P_k$ stops changing. That fixed point solves the algebraic Riccati equation, and gives one constant $K$: the infinite-horizon LQR you'll use most often.

Worked example: a scalar system

Take $x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k$ with $Q = 1$, $R = 1$. The steady-state Riccati equation is

$$P = 1 + P - \frac{P^2}{1 + P} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P^2 = 1 + P$$

so $P = (1 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618$ and $K = P/(1 + P) \approx 0.618$. The closed loop is $x_{k+1} = (1 - 0.618)\, x_k = 0.382\, x_k$: the error shrinks by 62% per step.

Raise effort cost to $R = 10$: now $P^2 - P - 10 = 0$, so $P \approx 3.70$, $K = P/(10 + P) \approx 0.27$, and the error shrinks only 27% per step. Gentler control, slower convergence.

Tuning with Q and R

Only the ratio of $Q$ to $R$ matters. Larger $Q$ entries push their states to zero faster; larger $R$ entries make the matching inputs smaller and smoother. A practical start is Bryson's rule: make each weight one over the square of the largest acceptable value, so $Q_{ii} = 1/x_{i,\max}^2$ and $R_{jj} = 1/u_{j,\max}^2$.

LQR needs the full state. If you only measure part of it, pair it with a Kalman filter; that combination is called LQG.

Common mistake: using an LQR gain far from where you linearized. $K$ is optimal for the linear model, and the linear model is only good near its operating point. A pendulum balancer designed at upright fails at 60 degrees.

In continuous time

The same story holds for $\dot x = Ax + Bu$ with cost $\int (x^\top Q x + u^\top R u)\, dt$. The gain is $K = R^{-1} B^\top P$, where $P$ solves

$$A^\top P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^\top P + Q = 0$$

The continuous and discrete gains are not interchangeable: design in the same time base your controller runs in. Libraries solve both versions in one call (for example, scipy.linalg.solve_continuous_are and solve_discrete_are).

trajectory_tracking.s: Close the loop around a planned trajectory so the robot follows it despite disturbances and model error.
i: Tracking controllers combine a feedforward input $u_d(t)$ from the plan with feedback on the error: $u = u_d(t) + K(x_d(t) - x)$.
Feedforward provides the input the model needs to follow the path; feedback corrects disturbances and model error, so neither alone suffices on a real robot.
For the unicycle, flatness supplies nominal $(x_d, y_d)$ and their derivatives, and a tracking law can set virtual accelerations from position and velocity errors and map them back to $(a, \omega)$.
q: A tracking controller uses only feedback $u = K(x_d - x)$ with no feedforward. On a curved path, what do you typically see?
Perfect tracking, since high-gain feedback removes all error
A persistent lag behind the reference, since some error is needed to generate the required input
Immediate instability, since feedback without feedforward is never stable
Exact tracking only if the path is curved rather than straight
Without feedforward the needed input must come from error, so the robot lags the moving reference. Pure feedback is not inherently unstable; it just tracks poorly.
trajectory_tracking.t: Simulate a 1D double integrator tracking $x_d = \sin t$ with $u = K_p e + K_d \dot e$, with and without the feedforward term $\ddot x_d = -\sin t$, and compare errors.
trajectory_tracking.T:
Why a plan isn't enough

Differential flatness gives you a planned path and the inputs that would follow it, if your model were perfect. Replay those inputs on a real robot and it drifts: wheel slip, a bump and a wrong mass all add up, and nothing pulls it back. Trajectory tracking closes the loop around the plan.

Feedforward plus feedback

Every good tracking controller has two parts:

$$u = \underbrace{u_d(t)}_{\text{feedforward: what the plan needs}} + \underbrace{K\,(x_d(t) - x)}_{\text{feedback: correct the error}}$$

Feedforward does most of the work. Without it, the controller only acts when there's already error, so it always lags behind a moving target. Feedback handles everything the model got wrong.

The book's tracker: PD in flat outputs

For the dynamically extended unicycle (state $(x, y, v, \theta)$, inputs $(a, \omega)$), flatness lets you write the position accelerations directly in terms of the inputs:

$$\begin{bmatrix} \ddot x \\ \ddot y \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -v\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & v\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}}_{J(\theta, v)} \begin{bmatrix} a \\ \omega \end{bmatrix}$$

So choose the accelerations you want, a "virtual input" $w$: the planned acceleration plus PD feedback on the position and velocity errors,

$$w_1 = \ddot x_d + k_p (x_d - x) + k_d (\dot x_d - \dot x), \qquad w_2 = \ddot y_d + k_p (y_d - y) + k_d (\dot y_d - \dot y)$$

and recover the real inputs with $(a, \omega) = J^{-1} w$. The tracking error then obeys $\ddot e + k_d\,\dot e + k_p\,e = 0$ in each direction, which decays to zero for any $k_p, k_d > 0$.

Worked example

Pick $k_p = 4$ and $k_d = 4$. The error equation $\ddot e + 4\dot e + 4e = 0$ has a repeated root at $-2$, so it's critically damped: no overshoot, and the error goes as $(c_1 + c_2 t)\,e^{-2t}$. A 1 m error that starts at rest is down to about 9 cm after 2 s and under 2 cm after 3 s. For the inversion, $\det J = v\cos^2\theta + v\sin^2\theta = v$, so $J$ is invertible whenever the robot is moving.

Common mistake: starting the tracker from rest. At $v = 0$, $\det J = 0$ and $J^{-1}$ doesn't exist. Start with a small nonzero speed, or switch to a different controller near stops.

ilqr.s: Repeatedly linearize about the current trajectory and solve an LQR problem, extending LQR to nonlinear systems.
i: iLQR rolls out the current inputs to get a nominal trajectory, linearizes dynamics and quadratizes cost along it, and solves a time-varying LQR problem for an update.
The backward pass produces feedforward terms k_t and feedback gains K_t; the forward pass applies u_t = ū_t + α k_t + K_t (x_t - x̄_t), with a line search on α.
DDP is the same idea but keeps second-order dynamics terms in the backward pass; iLQR drops them, making each iteration cheaper while still converging well in practice.
q: What distinguishes DDP from iLQR?
DDP uses a nonlinear dynamics model while iLQR requires linear dynamics
DDP produces only open-loop inputs while iLQR also produces feedback gains
DDP keeps second-order derivatives of the dynamics, which iLQR omits
DDP solves the problem forward in time while iLQR works backward

Both handle nonlinear dynamics with backward and forward passes, and both produce feedback gains; DDP adds the dynamics' second-order terms. iLQR linearizes nonlinear dynamics; it does not require them to be linear.

ilqr.T:
LQR for nonlinear systems, one linearization at a time

LQR needs linear dynamics and a quadratic cost. iLQR (iterative LQR) handles nonlinear $x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k)$ by repeating three steps:

  • Roll out the current inputs $\bar u_k$ through the real dynamics to get a nominal trajectory $\bar x_k$.
  • Approximate around it: linearize the dynamics and take a second-order expansion of the cost at every step.
  • Solve that time-varying LQR problem for a correction, apply it, and repeat until the cost stops improving.

Each pass is cheap, and the approximation gets better as the trajectory settles.

The local model

For small deviations $\delta x_k = x_k - \bar x_k$ and $\delta u_k = u_k - \bar u_k$, the dynamics become

$$\delta x_{k+1} \approx A_k\, \delta x_k + B_k\, \delta u_k, \qquad A_k = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big|_{\bar x_k, \bar u_k},\quad B_k = \frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\Big|_{\bar x_k, \bar u_k}$$

The cost gets the same treatment: gradients and Hessians of the step cost at each $(\bar x_k, \bar u_k)$. Unlike plain LQR, the model now includes linear terms, because the nominal trajectory isn't at the cost's minimum.

Backward pass, then forward pass

The backward pass runs a Riccati-like recursion from the last step to the first. At each step it produces a feedforward correction $k_k$ and a feedback gain $K_k$.

The forward pass simulates the true nonlinear dynamics with

$$u_k = \bar u_k + \alpha\, k_k + K_k (x_k - \bar x_k)$$

starting with $\alpha = 1$. If the new cost isn't lower, halve $\alpha$ and try again: a line search. The feedback term matters even during optimization, because it keeps the new rollout close to where the linear model is valid.

Worked example: one step

Take $x_{k+1} = x_k + 0.1 \sin x_k + u_k$ with $x_0 = 1$, cost $\tfrac12 u_0^2 + 5 x_1^2$, and initial guess $\bar u_0 = 0$.

  • Rollout: $\bar x_1 = 1 + 0.1 \sin 1 \approx 1.084$, cost $5 \times 1.084^2 \approx 5.88$.
  • Backward pass: the terminal cost has slope $10\,\bar x_1 \approx 10.84$ and curvature $10$; with $B_0 = 1$, the correction is $k_0 = -10.84/(1 + 10) \approx -0.986$.
  • Forward pass: $u_0 = -0.986$ gives $x_1 \approx 0.099$ and cost $\approx 0.53$.

With one step and fixed $x_0$, the dynamics are linear in $u$, so one iteration is exact. Over longer horizons the $\sin x$ term makes it take several.

iLQR versus DDP

DDP (differential dynamic programming) is the older, fuller version. It keeps second derivatives of the dynamics in the backward pass; iLQR drops them. iLQR iterations are cheaper and in practice converge almost as fast, so it's the usual choice. Both return a locally optimal trajectory plus the gains $K_k$, which you can keep as a tracking controller around it.

Common mistake: running iLQR without regularization. If the quadratic model isn't positive definite in $u$, the backward pass divides by a non-positive number and the step goes wild. Add $\mu I$ to that term, raising $\mu$ when a step fails and lowering it when steps succeed.

mpc.s: Re-solve a short-horizon trajectory optimization at every step and apply only the first input. Handles constraints explicitly.
i: MPC solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem from the current measured state at each step, applies only the first input, then shifts the horizon and repeats.
Constraints on inputs and states (actuator limits, obstacles) enter the optimization directly, which LQR and PID cannot do natively.
Re-solving from fresh measurements makes MPC a feedback controller; stability is usually encouraged with terminal costs or constraints, and computation time limits horizon length.
q: Why does MPC apply only the first input of each optimized sequence instead of executing the whole plan?
Because later inputs violate constraints and must be discarded
Because solvers return only one input per call
Because the cost function weights only the first step
Because re-solving from the newly measured state gives feedback against disturbances
Replanning from the measured state each step turns open-loop optimization into closed-loop control. All inputs in the sequence satisfy constraints; discarding them is about feedback, not feasibility.

mpc.T:
Plan, take one step, plan again

Model predictive control (MPC) turns trajectory optimization into feedback. At every control step:

  • Measure (or estimate) the current state $x(t)$.
  • Solve an optimal control problem over a short horizon of $N$ steps, starting from $x(t)$.
  • Apply only the first input $u_0$ of that plan, and throw the rest away.

At the next step the horizon slides forward by one and you solve again from a fresh measurement. That's why it's also called receding horizon control. Because each plan starts from what actually happened, disturbances and model errors get corrected.

The problem solved at every step

For a linear model the inner problem is usually

$$\min_{u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}} \; \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( x_k^\top Q x_k + u_k^\top R u_k \right) + x_N^\top P\, x_N$$

subject to $x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k$, $x_0 = x(t)$, $u_{\min} \le u_k \le u_{\max}$, and $x_k$ inside a safe set. With linear dynamics and constraints this is a quadratic program, which solvers handle in microseconds to milliseconds. With nonlinear dynamics it's a nonlinear program, often solved with a few SQP or iLQR iterations.

Why constraints are the selling point

LQR and PID don't know actuators have limits. When their command saturates, the robot does something the controller never planned for. MPC builds the limits into the plan, so it can, for example, start braking early because it knows braking force is limited, or slow down before a corner because it knows lateral acceleration is. Speed limits, joint limits, keep-out zones and actuator rates all go in the same way.

Worked example: a limit that binds, then doesn't

Take $x_{k+1} = x_k + u_k$, horizon $N = 3$, cost $\sum_{k=1}^{3} x_k^2 + \sum_{k=0}^{2} u_k^2$, and the limit $|u_k| \le 1$. Start at $x = 2.5$.

  • Without the limit, the best first move would be $u_0 \approx -1.54$, which isn't allowed.
  • With it, MPC plans $(-1, -0.9, -0.3)$ and applies $u_0 = -1$. The state becomes $1.5$.
  • Re-solving from $1.5$, the limit no longer binds: the new plan is about $(-0.92, -0.35, -0.12)$.

Notice the second step is $-0.92$, not the $-0.9$ planned a moment ago. MPC never commits to its old plan.

Horizon, stability and compute

A longer horizon sees trouble sooner but costs more to solve, and the solve must finish within one control period: a 20 Hz loop leaves 50 ms. The terminal cost $x_N^\top P x_N$ stands in for everything beyond the horizon; using the LQR cost-to-go $P$ is a common choice that helps make the closed loop stable.

Common mistake: making the horizon too short. A car whose plan covers only 1 s can't see that it needs 2 s to stop, and by the time the obstacle enters the horizon, no feasible plan is left. The horizon must cover the slowest thing the robot needs to anticipate.

config_space.s: Represent every possible robot pose as a point, with obstacles becoming forbidden regions. Planning becomes finding a path between points.
i: The configuration q of a robot is the minimal set of parameters that fixes the position of every point on it: (x, y) for a point robot, (x, y, θ) for a planar rigid body, joint angles for an arm.
Obstacles map into C-space as C_obs, the set of q where the robot body intersects an obstacle; C_free is the rest. For a disk robot of radius r, C_obs is each obstacle grown (Minkowski-summed) by r.
Planning a collision-free motion for a shaped robot becomes finding a continuous path for a single point from q_start to q_goal inside C_free, which lets one algorithm serve many robot shapes.
q: A circular mobile robot of radius 0.3 m moves in a 2D map. When you build its configuration space in (x, y), what happens to a 1 m wide wall?
It stays 1 m wide, since only the robot's center matters in C-space
It shrinks to 0.4 m wide, because the robot occupies part of the free space
It becomes 1.6 m wide, because the wall is grown by the robot radius on each side
It gains a third dimension, because a disk robot also needs a heading angle θ

C_obs is the set of center positions where the disk touches the wall, so the wall is inflated by 0.3 m on both sides. A disk is rotationally symmetric, so heading does not affect collision and (x, y) suffices.
config_space.t: Draw a square obstacle and a disk robot of radius r on paper, then sketch the C-space obstacle by sliding the disk around the square's boundary; note the rounded corners.
config_space.T:
One point per pose

A robot's configuration $q$ is the smallest set of numbers that fixes where every point of the robot is. The set of all configurations is the configuration space, or C-space.

  • A point robot on a floor: $q = (x, y)$, a 2-D C-space.
  • A rigid body moving in a plane: $q = (x, y, \theta)$, 3-D.
  • A 6-joint arm: the six joint angles, 6-D.

The dimension equals the robot's degrees of freedom. Moving the robot, however complicated its shape, becomes moving one point through this space.

Obstacles grow in C-space

An obstacle in the world becomes a forbidden region of C-space:

$$\mathcal{C}_{\text{obs}} = \{\, q : \text{the robot at } q \text{ overlaps an obstacle} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{C}_{\text{free}} = \mathcal{C} \setminus \mathcal{C}_{\text{obs}}$$

For a disk robot of radius $r$ described by its center, $\mathcal{C}_{\text{obs}}$ is every obstacle grown outward by $r$ (a Minkowski sum). The robot shrinks to a point and the obstacles swell to make up for it. A motion plan is then a continuous path from $q_{\text{start}}$ to $q_{\text{goal}}$ that stays in $\mathcal{C}_{\text{free}}$.

Worked example: will it fit through the door?

A round vacuum robot has radius $r = 0.3$ m.

  • A corridor 0.8 m wide: grow each wall by 0.3 m and the free strip for the robot's center is $0.8 - 2(0.3) = 0.2$ m wide. It fits, with 10 cm of slack on each side.
  • A gap 0.5 m wide between two chairs: $0.5 - 0.6 = -0.1$ m. In C-space the gap is closed. No planner will find a path through it, and none should.

Seeing this in C-space is instant; seeing it from the robot's outline usually needs a picture.

Rotation adds a dimension, and angles wrap

A rectangular robot fits through a gap sideways but not head-on, so whether $q$ is free depends on $\theta$ too. Its $\mathcal{C}_{\text{obs}}$ is a 3-D shape whose cross-section changes with heading.

Angles also wrap around: $\theta = 359°$ and $\theta = 1°$ are neighbors. So C-space isn't always a flat box. For a planar body it's a plane times a circle; for a two-joint arm with full rotation it's a torus.

Common mistake: measuring distance between angles without wrapping. A planner that thinks $359°$ and $1°$ are $358°$ apart will turn the long way round, or miss a path entirely.

Why the abstraction pays off

One planner now serves every robot: it only needs to ask "is $q$ in $\mathcal{C}_{\text{free}}$?" and "is the straight segment between two configurations free?". A collision checker answers both from the robot's geometry.

In 2-D or 3-D you can build $\mathcal{C}_{\text{obs}}$ explicitly, for example on a grid, and search it. For an arm with 6 or 7 joints that's hopeless, which is why high-dimensional planners sample configurations and check them one at a time instead.
