object_detection.s: Locate and label objects with bounding boxes, the input most downstream tracking and planning modules consume.
i: A detector outputs bounding boxes, class labels and confidence scores; boxes are compared with intersection over union (IoU), and accuracy is summarized by mean average precision (mAP).

Two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) propose regions then classify and refine them; one-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet) predict classes and box offsets densely from anchors or points in one pass.
Detectors produce many overlapping boxes per object, so non-maximum suppression keeps the highest-scoring box and removes others whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold.
q: Two boxes of size 10×10 overlap in a 5×10 region. What is their IoU, and will NMS with threshold 0.5 suppress the lower-scoring one?
IoU = 0.33, so neither box is suppressed
IoU = 0.5, so the lower-scoring box is suppressed
IoU = 0.33, so the lower-scoring box is suppressed
IoU = 0.25, so the lower-scoring box is suppressed
Intersection = 50, union = 100 + 100 - 50 = 150, IoU = 1/3, which is below 0.5, so both survive. The common mistake is dividing by one box area (giving 0.5).
object_detection.t: Write an iou(box_a, box_b) and a greedy NMS function in NumPy, and test them on 10 random jittered copies of the same box.
object_detection.T:
What a detector outputs

A classifier says what is in an image. A detector says what and where: a list of bounding boxes, each with a class label and a confidence score. For example, "pedestrian, 0.93, box from $(120, 80)$ to $(180, 240)$".

That list is what the rest of the stack consumes. Trackers follow the boxes over time, and planners treat them as obstacles to avoid. So a missed pedestrian or a phantom car flows straight into the robot's decisions.

Comparing boxes with IoU

To check a predicted box against the truth, or two predictions against each other, use intersection over union:

$$\text{IoU} = \frac{\text{area of overlap}}{\text{area of union}}$$

Two $4 \times 4$ boxes, one from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 4)$ and one from $(2, 2)$ to $(6, 6)$, overlap in a $2 \times 2$ square. The union is $16 + 16 - 4 = 28$, so $\text{IoU} = 4 / 28 \approx 0.14$. A prediction usually counts as correct if its IoU with a true box of the same class is at least $0.5$.

Two-stage and one-stage detectors

  • Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN first propose regions likely to contain objects, then classify each region and refine its box. They're accurate, but slower.
  • One-stage detectors such as YOLO, SSD and RetinaNet predict class scores and box offsets densely, for every cell of a feature map, in one pass. They're fast enough for real-time robots.

Many predict boxes relative to preset anchor boxes of typical shapes; newer anchor-free designs predict object centers and sizes directly.

Non-maximum suppression

A dense detector fires many overlapping boxes for each object. Non-maximum suppression (NMS) cleans them up:

  • Sort the boxes by score and keep the best one.
  • Delete every remaining box whose IoU with it is above a threshold, say $0.5$.
  • Repeat with the next-best remaining box.

Three boxes on one car, scored $0.9$, $0.8$ and $0.6$, with IoUs of $0.7$ and $0.6$ to the best, collapse to the $0.9$ box.

Measuring accuracy: mAP

As you lower the score threshold, the detector finds more true objects (higher recall) but also makes more false detections (lower precision). Average precision (AP) is the area under the precision–recall curve for one class; mAP averages it over classes. Benchmarks also state the IoU threshold, such as mAP@0.5, or an average over thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95.

Common mistake: an NMS threshold that is too low for crowds. Two pedestrians walking side by side can have boxes with IoU above $0.5$, and NMS deletes one of them. In crowded scenes, raise the threshold or use a detector that handles overlap.

detection_3d.s: Predict oriented 3D boxes from point clouds or voxels, which is what a planner needs to reason about other agents.
i: 3D detectors predict oriented boxes (x, y, z, length, width, height, yaw) plus class, which gives a planner the position, size and heading of agents in metric space.

Lidar-based methods operate on voxels or pillars (VoxelNet, SECOND, PointPillars) or directly on points; many use a bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation where objects rarely overlap and scale does not shrink with distance.
Camera-only 3D detection must infer depth from monocular cues or multi-view geometry and is less accurate in range; fusion with lidar or radar combines dense semantics with metric depth.
q: Why do many lidar 3D detectors convert features into a bird's-eye-view grid before predicting boxes?
Because lidar points cannot be represented in a perspective image
Because BEV removes the need to predict object heading
Because in BEV objects keep their metric size regardless of distance and seldom overlap, which simplifies box regression
Because BEV doubles the point cloud density at long range

On the ground plane, a car is the same size near or far and road agents rarely occlude each other from above, making detection heads easier to design. Heading must still be predicted, as the yaw parameter.
detection_3d.t: Project a synthetic lidar point cloud of two boxes onto a 0.2 m BEV occupancy grid in NumPy and plot max height per cell.
detection_3d.T:
What a planner needs from perception

A 2-D box in an image says where something appears, not where it is. A planner needs objects in metric space, so a 3-D detector outputs an oriented box for each object:

$$(x,\ y,\ z,\ l,\ w,\ h,\ \theta)$$

That's the center, the size (length, width, height), and the yaw $\theta$, the heading around the vertical axis, plus a class and a score. Many detectors also predict velocity. With this, a planner knows how far away a car is, how much room it takes up, and which way it's pointing.

Detecting in the lidar point cloud

Most accurate 3-D detectors use lidar. Typical pipelines turn the points into a grid with voxel or pillar networks (VoxelNet, SECOND, PointPillars), compress it to a 2-D feature map seen from above, and run a detection head on it. Anchor-based heads regress boxes from preset car or pedestrian shapes. Center-based heads such as CenterPoint predict a heatmap of object centers, then regress size and yaw at each peak.

Why the bird's-eye view works

Seen from above, objects on a road almost never overlap, and an object's size on the grid doesn't depend on its distance: a car is about $4.5 \times 1.8$ m whether it's 5 m or 50 m away. That's the opposite of a camera image, where far objects shrink and near ones hide others. The planner also reasons in this top-down view, so detections arrive in the form it needs.

Worked example: corners of a box

A car is detected at center $(10, 5)$ m with $l = 4.5$ m, $w = 1.8$ m and yaw $\theta = 30°$. Each corner is the center plus the rotated half-size offset $(\pm l/2,\ \pm w/2) = (\pm 2.25,\ \pm 0.9)$. For the front-left corner:

$$x = 10 + 2.25\cos 30° - 0.9 \sin 30° \approx 11.50, \qquad y = 5 + 2.25 \sin 30° + 0.9 \cos 30° \approx 6.90$$

The other corners are $(12.40, 5.35)$, $(8.50, 3.10)$ and $(7.60, 4.65)$. Collision checks use these four points.

Cameras, and fusing sensors

Camera-only 3-D detection must infer depth, from object size, from where an object meets the ground, or from several overlapping cameras. It's cheap and sees color and texture, but depth error grows quickly with range. Lidar gives precise depth but is sparse at long range and sees no color. Radar measures speed directly and works in rain and fog. Fusion combines them, either by merging each sensor's detections or by merging features inside the network.

Common mistake: ignoring the 180° heading ambiguity. A box with yaw $\theta$ and one with $\theta + 180°$ cover exactly the same space, so the box IoU looks perfect, but a tracker reading the heading predicts the car driving backwards. Check heading separately.

segmentation.s: Label every pixel or point by class, and separate individual objects of the same class.
i: Semantic segmentation assigns a class to every pixel; instance segmentation also separates individual objects of the same class; panoptic segmentation combines both for 'stuff' and 'things'.

Fully convolutional networks with encoder-decoder structure (FCN, U-Net with skip connections, DeepLab with dilated convolutions) recover per-pixel predictions at full resolution while using deep context.
Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN with a small mask head per detected box, giving instance masks; accuracy is measured with per-class IoU, averaged as mIoU.
q: A semantic segmentation output labels a group of three touching pedestrians as one 'person' region. What extra capability would separate them?
Higher input image resolution
A larger number of semantic classes
A loss function that weights rare classes more
Instance segmentation, which assigns a distinct identity to each object

Semantic labels only say 'person' per pixel, with no notion of which person; instance segmentation (e.g. Mask R-CNN) assigns each pedestrian its own mask. Resolution helps boundaries but not identity.
segmentation.t: Given a NumPy array of predicted and ground-truth label maps, write a function computing per-class IoU and mIoU, and test it on a small hand-made 6×6 example.
segmentation.T:
Three kinds of segmentation

Detection draws boxes; segmentation labels pixels (or lidar points).

  • Semantic segmentation gives every pixel a class: road, sidewalk, car, person, sky. Two people touching get one merged "person" region.
  • Instance segmentation separates individual objects: person 1, person 2, each with its own mask.
  • Panoptic segmentation does both. Countable things (cars, people) get instance masks, and amorphous stuff (road, grass, sky) gets class labels.

For robots, segmentation gives drivable area, free floor space, and the exact outline of obstacles, which a box can't.

Encoder–decoder networks

A classification CNN shrinks the image as it goes, trading resolution for context. Segmentation needs both: enough context to know a pixel is part of a car, and full resolution to place the car's edge.

  • Encoder–decoder networks shrink, then upsample back to full size.
  • U-Net adds skip connections that copy fine detail from each encoder level to the matching decoder level.
  • DeepLab uses dilated convolutions, kernels with gaps, to see a wide area without shrinking the feature map.

Instance masks with Mask R-CNN

Mask R-CNN builds instance segmentation on top of detection. It is Faster R-CNN plus a small extra head: for each detected box, a tiny fully convolutional network predicts a mask, typically $28 \times 28$, over just that box, which is then resized to the box's size in the image. Detection separates the instances; the mask head outlines each one.

Worked example: measuring with IoU

For each class, compare predicted pixels with the true ones. Say the true road covers 10,000 pixels, the prediction covers 9,000, and 8,500 of them overlap:

$$\text{IoU}_{\text{road}} = \frac{8500}{9000 + 10000 - 8500} = \frac{8500}{10500} \approx 0.81$$

The mIoU is the mean of this over all classes. Every class counts equally, so a model that is great on road but misses pedestrians gets a poor score.

Why not just count correct pixels?

Pixel accuracy, the fraction of pixels labeled correctly, is dominated by the big classes. If road and sky fill 90% of every image, a model that never finds a single pedestrian can still score above 90%. For a robot, the small classes, such as people, cyclists and curbs, are often the ones that matter most.

Common mistake: reporting pixel accuracy, or a single averaged number, and calling the model good. Always check per-class IoU for the classes that matter to safety. A large average can hide a class the model barely detects.

bayes_filter.s: Maintain a belief over state with two alternating steps: predict with the motion model, correct with the measurement.
i: The belief $\mathrm{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t})$ is a full probability distribution over the state, not a single guess, so it captures both the estimate and its uncertainty.
Predict: $\overline{\mathrm{bel}}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\, \mathrm{bel}(x_{t-1})\, dx_{t-1}$ spreads the belief through the motion model, which typically increases uncertainty.

Correct: $\mathrm{bel}(x_t) = \eta\, p(z_t \mid x_t)\, \overline{\mathrm{bel}}(x_t)$ reweights by the measurement likelihood and renormalizes; recursion works because of the Markov assumption on state and measurements.
q: A robot runs a Bayes filter but its sensor fails, so for many steps it only executes the predict step. What happens to its belief?
It stays exactly as it was after the last correction step
It collapses onto the single most likely state over time
It generally spreads out as motion noise accumulates each step
It becomes uniform immediately after the first missed update
Each prediction convolves the belief with noisy motion, so uncertainty grows without measurements to shrink it. It does not freeze, and it does not jump to uniform in one step; it diffuses gradually.
bayes_filter.t: For a door/no-door world with prior $P(\text{door}) = 0.3$, sensor $P(z = \text{door} \mid \text{door}) = 0.6$ and $P(z = \text{door} \mid \text{no door}) = 0.2$, compute the posterior after one 'door' reading by hand, then after two readings.
bayes_filter.T:
Keep a belief, not a guess

A robot never knows exactly where it is. Instead of one best guess, the Bayes filter keeps a belief: a probability for every possible state, given everything it has done and seen so far,

$$\mathrm{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t})$$

where $u$ are the controls (what it commanded) and $z$ are the measurements. A sharp belief means "I'm fairly sure"; a spread-out one means "I could be in several places".

Two steps, repeated forever

Predict. When the robot moves, push the belief through the motion model. Motion is noisy, so the belief spreads out:

$$\overline{\mathrm{bel}}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\, \mathrm{bel}(x_{t-1})\, dx_{t-1}$$

Correct. When a measurement arrives, reweight every state by how well it explains that measurement, then renormalize so the probabilities sum to one ($\eta$ is that normalizer):

$$\mathrm{bel}(x_t) = \eta\, p(z_t \mid x_t)\, \overline{\mathrm{bel}}(x_t)$$

This works step by step, without replaying history, because of the Markov assumption: the current state holds everything the past can tell you about the future.

The book's hallway

A robot drives along a hallway with doors and a sensor that looks for a door. Moving smears its belief forward; seeing a door sharpens the belief around positions next to doors. In a hallway with several identical doors, the belief can have several peaks at once, which the Bayes filter represents fine, and which a single Gaussian (next lesson) can't.

Worked example: one door, two readings

Before sensing, the robot thinks it's in front of a door with probability $P(\text{door}) = 0.5$. Its sensor says "door" with probability $0.6$ when there is one, and falsely with probability $0.2$ when there isn't. It reads "door":

$$P(\text{door} \mid z) = \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.2 \times 0.5} = \frac{0.30}{0.40} = 0.75$$

A second "door" reading (without moving) uses $0.75$ as the new prior:

$$\frac{0.6 \times 0.75}{0.6 \times 0.75 + 0.2 \times 0.25} = \frac{0.45}{0.50} = 0.9$$

Each reading is weak on its own; together they get the robot to 90% sure.

Common mistake: forgetting to normalize. Multiplying by the likelihood gives 0.30 and 0.10, not probabilities. Dividing by their sum (the $\eta$) is what turns them into 0.75 and 0.25.

histogram_filter.s: Run the Bayes filter over a grid of possible states. Exact but limited to small spaces.
i: The state space is partitioned into cells, and the belief is a vector of probabilities, one per cell, that sums to 1.

Prediction becomes a matrix-vector product (or a convolution for shift-invariant motion) with the transition probabilities; correction is elementwise multiplication by the likelihood followed by normalization.
It can represent any multimodal belief exactly up to discretization, but memory and compute grow exponentially with state dimension, so it suits 1-D to 3-D problems.
q: You switch a 2-D grid localizer (x, y at 10 cm cells) to also track heading in 5-degree bins. Roughly what happens to the cost per update?
It grows by about 72 times, since every (x, y) cell now has 72 heading cells
It grows by about 72 cells total, since heading is one extra axis
It is unchanged, because heading is folded into the motion model
It halves, because heading information sharpens the belief
Grid size is the product of bins along each dimension, so adding a 72-bin axis multiplies the cell count by 72. Treating it as additive is the tempting mistake that hides the curse of dimensionality.
histogram_filter.t: In NumPy, make a 1-D circular corridor of 20 cells with doors at 3 positions; implement predict as np.roll plus a small blur kernel and correct with a door sensor, and watch the belief go from multimodal to unimodal.

kalman_filter.s: The Bayes filter in closed form when dynamics are linear and noise is Gaussian.
i: With $x_t = A x_{t-1} + B u_t + \epsilon_t$, $\epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q)$, and $z_t = C x_t + \delta_t$, $\delta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)$, a Gaussian belief stays Gaussian, so the filter only tracks a mean $\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$.
Predict: $\bar\mu = A\mu + Bu$, $\bar\Sigma = A\Sigma A^\top + Q$. Update: $K = \bar\Sigma C^\top (C\bar\Sigma C^\top + R)^{-1}$, $\mu = \bar\mu + K(z - C\bar\mu)$, $\Sigma = (I - KC)\bar\Sigma$.
The gain $K$ weighs prediction against measurement: large $R$ (noisy sensor) shrinks $K$ toward trusting the model, small $R$ pushes the estimate toward the measurement.
q: In a Kalman filter you increase the measurement noise covariance $R$ while keeping $Q$ fixed. What is the effect on the update?
The gain grows, so the estimate follows measurements more closely
The posterior covariance after the update becomes smaller
The predicted covariance $A\Sigma A^\top + Q$ becomes larger
The gain shrinks, so the estimate relies more on the prediction
$K = \bar\Sigma C^\top (C\bar\Sigma C^\top + R)^{-1}$ decreases as $R$ grows, so measurements are trusted less and posterior covariance shrinks less. $R$ does not enter the prediction step at all.
kalman_filter.t: Write a 1-D Kalman filter for a constant-position model ($A = 1$, $C = 1$) with $Q = 0.01$ and $R = 1$; feed it noisy readings of a constant and plot how $K$ converges to a steady-state value.
kalman_filter.T:
The Bayes filter, made cheap

A full belief over every possible state is expensive. The Kalman filter makes three assumptions so the belief is always a Gaussian, described by just a mean $\mu$ and a covariance $\Sigma$:

  • the motion model is linear: $x_t = A x_{t-1} + B u_t + \epsilon_t$, with process noise $\epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q)$
  • the measurement model is linear: $z_t = C x_t + \delta_t$, with sensor noise $\delta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)$
  • the starting belief is Gaussian.

Under those assumptions a Gaussian stays Gaussian through both steps, and the filter is exact.

Predict

Move the mean with the model, and grow the uncertainty by the process noise:

$$\bar\mu = A\mu + Bu, \qquad \bar\Sigma = A \Sigma A^\top + Q$$

Update

Compare the measurement with what you expected to see, and correct by a fraction $K$ of the difference:

$$K = \bar\Sigma C^\top (C \bar\Sigma C^\top + R)^{-1}, \qquad \mu = \bar\mu + K(z - C\bar\mu), \qquad \Sigma = (I - KC)\bar\Sigma$$

The Kalman gain $K$ is the inverse-variance weighting from the measurement-noise lesson, in matrix form. A noisy sensor (large $R$) gives a small $K$: trust the model. A confident sensor gives a large $K$: follow the measurement.

Worked example: one dimension

A robot holds still ($A = 1$, $B = 0$, $C = 1$). Its belief is $\mu = 0$, $\Sigma = 1$. The model allows a little drift, $Q = 0.01$, and the sensor has $R = 1$. It measures $z = 0.8$.

  • Predict: $\bar\mu = 0$, $\bar\Sigma = 1 + 0.01 = 1.01$.
  • Gain: $K = \dfrac{1.01}{1.01 + 1} \approx 0.50$.
  • Update: $\mu = 0 + 0.50 \times 0.8 \approx 0.40$ and $\Sigma = (1 - 0.50) \times 1.01 \approx 0.50$.

Prediction and measurement were equally trusted, so the estimate lands halfway, and the uncertainty halves.

For moving robots the book uses a constant-velocity model, $x = (p, v)$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \Delta t \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$: you measure only position, and the filter still estimates velocity.

Common mistake: setting $Q$ to zero because "my model is right". Then $\bar\Sigma$ shrinks every step, $K$ goes to zero, and the filter stops listening to its sensors. A small $Q$ keeps it honest.

ekf_ukf.s: Extend the Kalman filter to nonlinear systems, by linearizing (EKF) or by propagating sigma points (UKF).
i: The EKF linearizes nonlinear $f$ and $h$ at the current mean using Jacobians $F = \partial f/\partial x$ and $H = \partial h/\partial x$, then applies the standard Kalman covariance equations with those matrices.
The UKF instead picks $2n+1$ sigma points that match the mean and covariance, pushes each through the true nonlinear function, and recomputes a weighted mean and covariance.
Both still assume a unimodal Gaussian belief; the UKF is typically more accurate for strong nonlinearities and needs no Jacobians, but neither can represent multimodal beliefs.
q: A system has a strongly curved measurement function, and the EKF's estimate becomes overconfident and drifts. Why might a UKF help here?
It replaces the Gaussian belief with a set of weighted particles
It captures the curvature by passing points through the true nonlinearity
It computes exact Jacobians instead of numerical approximations
It avoids the prediction step and only uses the measurement update

The UKF propagates sigma points through the actual nonlinear function, capturing mean and covariance more accurately (to second order) than a first-order linearization. It is still Gaussian, not a particle method.
ekf_ukf.t: Take $x \sim \mathcal{N}(1, 0.5^2)$ and $y = x^2$. Compare the EKF estimate of $E[y]$ ($f(\mu) = 1$) with a Monte Carlo estimate from 100k samples (true value $1.25$) and with a 3-point unscented transform.
ekf_ukf.T:
When the model isn't linear

Real robots are nonlinear: the unicycle has $\cos\theta$ in it, and a range sensor has a square root. Push a Gaussian through a nonlinear function and what comes out isn't Gaussian any more. Two fixes keep the Kalman filter's machinery:

$$x_t = f(x_{t-1}, u_t) + \epsilon_t, \qquad z_t = h(x_t) + \delta_t$$

The EKF: linearize at the mean

The extended Kalman filter uses the linearization lesson. At the current mean, replace $f$ and $h$ by their Jacobians,

$$F = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\bigg|_{\mu}, \qquad H = \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\bigg|_{\bar\mu}$$

and run the usual equations: $\bar\mu = f(\mu, u)$ and $\bar\Sigma = F\Sigma F^\top + Q$; then $K = \bar\Sigma H^\top(H\bar\Sigma H^\top + R)^{-1}$ and $\mu = \bar\mu + K(z - h(\bar\mu))$. The mean goes through the true nonlinear functions; only the covariance uses the straight-line approximation.

The UKF: push a few points through

The unscented Kalman filter skips the Jacobians. It picks $2n + 1$ sigma points (for an $n$-dimensional state) that have exactly the belief's mean and covariance, sends each one through the true nonlinear function, and computes a weighted mean and covariance of the results. It captures curvature that a straight-line approximation misses.

Worked example: $y = x^2$

Take $x \sim \mathcal{N}(1, 0.5^2)$ and $y = x^2$. The true mean is $E[y] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2 = 1.25$.

  • EKF: $E[y] \approx f(\mu) = 1$. It misses by 0.25 because it ignores the curve.
  • UKF (one dimension, scaling $\kappa = 2$): sigma points at $1$ and $1 \pm \sqrt{3 \times 0.25} \approx 1 \pm 0.866$, with weights $\tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac16, \tfrac16$. Squaring them gives $1$, $3.482$ and $0.018$, and
$$\tfrac23 \times 1 + \tfrac16 \times (3.482 + 0.018) = 0.667 + 0.583 = 1.25$$

which is exact.

Both are still a single Gaussian, so neither can say "I'm in one of two hallways". For that you need particles (Monte Carlo localization).

Common mistake: linearizing far from the truth. If the EKF's mean is badly off, its Jacobians describe the wrong part of the curve and the filter can grow overconfident and diverge. A good initial estimate matters.

particle_filter.s: Represent the belief with weighted samples, which handles multimodal and non-Gaussian distributions.
i: The belief is approximated by M samples x^[m] with weights w^[m]; more particles give a better approximation of arbitrary, including multimodal, distributions.
Each step samples every particle from the motion model, sets weight w^[m] proportional to p(z_t | x^[m]), then resamples particles with probability proportional to weight.
Resampling focuses particles in likely regions but causes particle deprivation; low-variance resampling and resampling only when effective sample size 1/Σ w^2 is low reduce this.
q: A particle filter uses a very accurate sensor (tiny measurement noise) and a modest number of particles. What failure is most likely?
The weights stay nearly uniform, so the sensor is effectively ignored
Particles collapse into a Gaussian and lose multimodality gracefully
Almost all weight lands on one or two particles, so diversity collapses
The motion model becomes linear, so a Kalman filter would be exact

A very peaked likelihood gives nearly zero weight to particles not almost exactly at the true state, so after resampling only a few survive (degeneracy). Inflating the measurement noise or adding particles helps.
particle_filter.t: Implement a 1-D particle filter with 200 particles tracking a random walk; print the effective sample size 1/Σ w^2 each step and compare resampling every step versus only when it drops below 100.

motion_measurement_models.s: Odometry and range-bearing models written as probability distributions, ready to plug into a filter.
i: A probabilistic motion model $p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})$ gives a distribution over the next pose; the odometry model decomposes motion into rotation, translation, rotation, each corrupted by noise.
A range-bearing sensor model predicts $r = \sqrt{(m_x - x)^2 + (m_y - y)^2}$ and $\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(m_y - y,\ m_x - x) - \theta$, with additive Gaussian noise, giving $p(z \mid x, m)$.
Sampling from the motion model naturally produces the curved 'banana' distribution that a Gaussian over $(x, y, \theta)$ cannot capture well, because heading uncertainty bends the position spread.
q: A robot with noisy heading drives straight 5 m. If you sample many end poses from its odometry motion model, what shape does the $(x, y)$ cloud take?
A crescent arc, because heading error maps into sideways displacement
A circle centered on the commanded end point with equal spread
A thin line along the direction of travel only
A single point, since odometry measures the motion exactly
Small heading errors rotate the whole displacement, sweeping points along an arc of radius about 5 m, creating a banana shape. A round blob would only arise if errors were independent in x and y.
motion_measurement_models.t: Sample 1000 end poses for a robot starting at the origin driving 5 m with heading noise of 0.1 rad and distance noise of 0.1 m; scatter-plot x versus y and observe the arc.
motion_measurement_models.T:
Two models every filter needs

The Bayes filter asks two questions: where could I be after this motion, $p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})$, and how likely is this reading from here, $p(z_t \mid x_t, m)$, given the map $m$. This lesson builds both for a robot moving in the plane.

The motion model: odometry, plus noise

Odometry reports how the robot moved between two poses. A standard way to write any planar move is as three pieces: turn by $\delta_{\text{rot1}}$, drive straight $\delta_{\text{trans}}$, turn by $\delta_{\text{rot2}}$. Each piece gets its own noise, larger for bigger moves. To sample from the model, perturb the three pieces and apply them; to get the probability of a pose, ask how far its pieces are from the reported ones.

The banana

Heading noise is what bends the distribution. Drive 5 m with a heading error of $\pm 0.1$ rad and the end point swings sideways by about $5 \times 0.1 = 0.5$ m, while distance noise only stretches it forwards and backwards. Sample many end points and they form a curved crescent, the "banana", not a round blob. A single Gaussian in $(x, y, \theta)$ can only approximate it.

The measurement model: range and bearing

A robot at pose $(x, y, \theta)$ sees a landmark $m_j$ at $(m_{j,x}, m_{j,y})$. A range-bearing sensor (lidar picking out a pole, a camera detecting a sign) reports

$$r = \sqrt{(m_{j,x} - x)^2 + (m_{j,y} - y)^2}, \qquad \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(m_{j,y} - y,\ m_{j,x} - x) - \theta$$

plus Gaussian noise $\delta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, R)$. The bearing is measured relative to where the robot faces, which is why $\theta$ is subtracted.

Worked example

The robot is at $(1, 1)$ facing $\theta = 0$, and a landmark is at $(4, 5)$. The offsets are $3$ and $4$, so

$$r = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\ \text{m}, \qquad \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(4, 3) \approx 0.93\ \text{rad} \approx 53^\circ$$

If the robot turns to face $\theta = 0.5$ rad without moving, the range stays 5 m and the bearing drops to about $0.43$ rad.

Common mistake: adding independent noise to $x$ and $y$. That gives a round blob and misses how heading error turns into sideways error. Put the noise on the turn and the distance, the way the robot actually moves.

ekf_localization.s: Estimate the robot's pose in a known map by fusing odometry with landmark measurements.
i: The state is the pose $(x, y, \theta)$ with a known landmark map; prediction uses the motion model with its Jacobian $F$ with respect to the state, and process noise $Q$.

Each landmark observation $z = h(x, m_j) + \delta$ is linearized with $H = \partial h/\partial x$, and the innovation $z - h(\bar\mu)$ updates the pose; bearing innovations must be wrapped to $(-\pi, \pi]$.
It requires known data association (which landmark was seen) and a reasonably good initial pose; a wrong association or huge initial error can make it diverge.
q: An EKF localizer receives a bearing measurement of 179 degrees while it predicted -179 degrees. If the innovation is not angle-wrapped, what happens?
Nothing much, since the Kalman gain automatically handles angles
The update is ignored because the innovation exceeds the gate
The covariance grows instead of shrinking for that update
It sees a 358 degree error and yanks the pose estimate far off
The true difference is only 2 degrees, but the raw subtraction gives 358 degrees, producing a huge, wrong correction. The gain does not know about angle periodicity; you must wrap the innovation.
ekf_localization.t: Write the $2 \times 3$ Jacobian $H$ of the range-bearing model with respect to $(x, y, \theta)$ for a landmark at $(m_x, m_y)$, then verify it numerically with finite differences at one pose.
ekf_localization.T:
The goal

You know the map: a list of landmarks $m_1, \ldots, m_N$ at known positions. You don't know the robot's pose $x = (x, y, \theta)$. EKF localization tracks the pose as a Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$ with the EKF from two lessons ago, using the motion and range-bearing models from the last lesson.

The loop (the book's Algorithm 2)

Predict with the motion model and its Jacobian $F$:

$$\bar\mu = f(\mu, u), \qquad \bar\Sigma = F \Sigma F^\top + Q$$

Correct once for each landmark $j$ you saw:

$$S = H \bar\Sigma H^\top + R, \qquad K = \bar\Sigma H^\top S^{-1}, \qquad \bar\mu \leftarrow \bar\mu + K\,(z - h(\bar\mu, m_j)), \qquad \bar\Sigma \leftarrow (I - KH)\bar\Sigma$$

where $H$ is the Jacobian of the range-bearing model at the predicted pose. Because the measurements are independent given the pose, doing them one after another gives the same answer as all at once.

The Jacobian you'll actually compute

With $\Delta x = m_{j,x} - \bar x$, $\Delta y = m_{j,y} - \bar y$ and $q = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2$:

$$H = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{\Delta x}{\sqrt q} & -\dfrac{\Delta y}{\sqrt q} & 0 \\[2mm] \dfrac{\Delta y}{q} & -\dfrac{\Delta x}{q} & -1 \end{bmatrix}$$

The first row says moving toward the landmark shortens the range; the last entry says turning left by some angle decreases the bearing by the same angle.

Worked example

Predicted pose $(1, 1, 0)$, landmark at $(4, 5)$: $\Delta x = 3$, $\Delta y = 4$, $q = 25$, so

$$H = \begin{bmatrix} -0.6 & -0.8 & 0 \\ 0.16 & -0.12 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Now the sensor reads a bearing of $179^\circ$ when the filter expected $-179^\circ$. The raw innovation is $358^\circ$; wrapped into $(-\pi, \pi]$ it's $-2^\circ$, a tiny correction instead of a wild one.

What it needs

EKF localization assumes data association: you know which landmark each measurement came from. The book's version for unknown associations picks, for each measurement, the landmark that makes it most likely under the predicted belief. It also needs a decent starting guess; if you don't know where you are at all, use Monte Carlo localization.

Common mistake: skipping the angle wrap. Without it, one reading near $\pm 180^\circ$ yanks the pose estimate far off, and the filter may never recover.

mcl.s: Particle-filter localization that can recover from being lost or placed at an unknown starting pose.
i: Monte Carlo localization is a particle filter over robot pose in a known map: sample motion, weight by p(z | x, map) such as a likelihood-field or beam model, then resample.
Initializing particles uniformly over free space solves global localization, since the filter can represent many hypotheses until measurements disambiguate them.
To recover from kidnapping or particle collapse, inject a small fraction of random particles, as in augmented MCL, when average measurement likelihood drops suddenly.
q: A robot running MCL is picked up and moved to another room (kidnapped). All particles are clustered at the old pose. What change lets it recover?
Increase measurement noise so all particles get equal weight
Inject random particles when measurement likelihood drops
Switch the motion model to a deterministic odometry update
Resample less often so the old cluster spreads out

With no particles near the true pose, the filter cannot find it; injecting random particles gives it hypotheses there. Just flattening weights or resampling less does not create particles in the new room.
mcl.t: On a 1-D corridor of length 10 with doors at 2, 5, and 8, run MCL with particles initialized uniformly; plot the particle histogram after each door sighting as the robot moves right.

ekf_slam.s: Add landmark positions to the state so the robot estimates its pose and the map together.
i: The state stacks the robot pose and all landmark positions, e.g. [x, y, θ, m1x, m1y, ..., mNx, mNy], with a full joint covariance of size (3+2N)².
Correlations between robot and landmarks are essential: observing one landmark again also corrects other correlated landmarks, which is why loop closure shrinks the whole map uncertainty.
Each update costs O(N²) due to the dense covariance, and it is sensitive to wrong data association and linearization errors, limiting it to a few hundred landmarks.
q: In EKF SLAM, a robot returns to re-observe the first landmark it mapped after a long loop. Why do landmarks it has not seen for a while also become more certain?
Their estimates are correlated with the robot and that landmark, so the update spreads
The filter resets every landmark covariance to its initial value on loop closure
Unseen landmarks are removed from the state, so their uncertainty is zero
The motion model is reapplied backward along the trajectory

The joint covariance carries cross-correlations built up while landmarks were observed from the drifting robot, so correcting the robot pose propagates to them. EKF SLAM does not re-run motion backward; that is closer to smoothing.
ekf_slam.t: For a robot with 3 pose states and 50 landmarks, compute the size of the covariance matrix and how many numbers it stores; then estimate how this scales if you map 5000 landmarks.

slam_front_end.s: The perception side of SLAM: extract features, associate them with landmarks, reject outliers, and detect loop closures before any estimation runs.
i: The front end turns raw sensor data into abstract constraints: detect and describe features (e.g. ORB keypoints), match them or register scans (ICP), and output relative pose measurements.
Data association decides which observation corresponds to which landmark; gating by Mahalanobis distance and RANSAC on geometric models reject outliers before they reach the estimator.
Loop closure detection recognizes a previously visited place (e.g. via bag-of-words appearance matching); a single false loop closure can badly warp the map, so verification is critical.
q: A SLAM system's map suddenly folds two separate corridors onto each other. Which front-end failure is the most likely cause?
The motion model noise covariance was set slightly too large
The back-end optimizer ran too few iterations to converge
A false loop closure linked two similar-looking places as one
Too few features were tracked between consecutive frames
A wrong loop closure adds a confident constraint saying two distinct places coincide, and the optimizer bends the map to satisfy it. Few features or loose noise cause drift, not a sudden fold.
slam_front_end.t: Generate 20 2-D point correspondences under a known rotation and translation, corrupt 6 with random outliers, and fit the transform with a simple RANSAC loop using 2-point samples and SVD.

pose_graph_slam.s: Treat poses as graph nodes and measurements as constraints, then solve for the configuration that best satisfies them all. Standard in modern SLAM.
i: Nodes are robot poses (and optionally landmarks); edges are relative measurements z_ij with information matrices Ω_ij from odometry, scan matching, or loop closures.
The estimate minimizes Σ e_ij^T Ω_ij e_ij, where e_ij is the error between measured and predicted relative pose, a nonlinear least squares problem solved by Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt.
The resulting system is sparse because each factor touches few variables, so sparse solvers scale to large maps; unlike filtering, it re-linearizes past poses, reducing linearization error.
q: Why does a pose-graph solver typically produce a more accurate map than EKF SLAM after a loop closure on a long trajectory?
It assumes measurements have no noise, so constraints are exact
It only keeps the current pose, so old errors are forgotten
It replaces the Gaussian error model with a uniform one
It re-linearizes all past poses during optimization

A filter linearizes once and marginalizes past poses, freezing linearization errors, whereas smoothing re-linearizes the whole trajectory around better estimates each iteration. It still models noise via information matrices.
pose_graph_slam.t: Build a 1-D pose graph with poses x0..x4, odometry edges of +1.0 each, a loop edge x4 - x0 = 3.6, and x0 fixed at 0; solve the linear least squares with NumPy and see how the error is distributed.

sensor_fusion.s: Combine sensors with different rates and error profiles, such as IMU with GPS, into one consistent estimate.
i: Fusion combines sensors with complementary errors: an IMU is high-rate but drifts when integrated, while GPS is low-rate and noisy but drift-free, so together they give smooth, bounded error.
A common design uses the IMU to drive the prediction step at high rate and applies each GPS fix as a measurement update whenever it arrives, handling different rates naturally.
Correct fusion needs time-synchronized data, known extrinsic calibration between sensors, and honest noise covariances; overconfident R or Q makes the filter inconsistent.
q: In an IMU+GPS Kalman filter, GPS drops out for 30 seconds in a tunnel. What should you expect from the estimate during the outage?
It freezes at the last GPS fix until a new one arrives
It keeps updating from IMU, with covariance and drift growing
It becomes more certain because IMU noise is lower than GPS noise
It diverges immediately because the measurement update is missing
Without GPS, the filter keeps predicting with integrated IMU data, so error accumulates and the covariance grows until GPS returns. It neither freezes nor fails instantly.
sensor_fusion.t: Simulate 1-D motion with a noisy biased accelerometer at 100 Hz and noisy position fixes at 1 Hz; compare dead-reckoned position with a Kalman filter fusing both, including a 20 s gap without fixes.

object_tracking.s: Follow detected objects over time, deciding which new detection belongs to which existing track.
i: Each track has its own filter (often a Kalman filter with a constant-velocity model) that predicts where the object will be when the next detections arrive.

Data association matches detections to tracks, e.g. by gating with Mahalanobis distance and solving the assignment with the Hungarian algorithm on a cost matrix; JPDA and MHT handle ambiguity probabilistically.
Track management births tracks from unmatched detections and deletes tracks that go unmatched for several frames, trading false tracks against missed objects.
q: Two pedestrians cross paths and briefly occlude each other. Why is greedy nearest-neighbor association likely to swap their identities?
It ignores predicted motion and joint consistency, picking locally closest pairs
It uses the Mahalanobis distance, which ignores track covariance
It deletes both tracks the moment one detection is missing
It requires a nonlinear motion model that pedestrians do not follow

Greedy local choices at the crossing can assign each detection to the wrong track; global assignment using predicted velocity and uncertainty, or multi-hypothesis methods, are more robust. Mahalanobis distance actually does use covariance.
object_tracking.t: Given 3 track predictions and 3 detections in 2-D, build the 3x3 Euclidean cost matrix and solve it with scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment; then perturb one detection to see when the assignment flips.

learned_fusion.s: Fuse sensors inside a network, for example in a bird's-eye-view feature space, then hand the result to classical filters. Where the classical and learned halves of the stack meet.
i: Learned fusion maps camera images and lidar points into a shared bird's-eye-view grid where features from all sensors are aligned in metric ground coordinates.
Camera-to-BEV lifting predicts depth or uses attention (e.g. transformer queries over image features) to place image features in 3-D, since a single image lacks direct depth.

The network outputs detections or occupancy with uncertainty, which classical trackers and filters then consume; mid-level feature fusion often beats fusing final detections, but it needs calibrated sensors and lots of data.
q: A BEV fusion network trained with a fixed camera-lidar calibration is deployed on a car where the camera mount shifted slightly. What is the most likely effect?
None, because learned features are invariant to calibration
The tracker downstream automatically re-estimates the calibration
Camera features land in wrong BEV cells, degrading fused output
Only lidar performance drops, since lidar points are reprojected

Projection into BEV relies on extrinsics, so a mount shift misplaces camera features relative to lidar and degrades detections. Networks are not automatically invariant, and a standard tracker does not recalibrate sensors.
learned_fusion.t: Take a pinhole camera with focal length 500 px at height 1.5 m looking level; compute where a ground point 10 m ahead projects in the image, then how far it moves in BEV if the pitch is off by 1 degree.

fsm.s: Hand-designed modes and transitions that sequence behaviors. Still how many deployed robots decide what to do next.
i: A finite state machine has a set of discrete modes (e.g. EXPLORE, APPROACH, GRASP, RECOVER), each running a behavior, and transitions triggered by events or conditions.
FSMs are transparent and easy to verify by inspection, which is why they sequence behaviors in many deployed robots; each transition can be logged and tested.
They scale poorly: the number of states and transitions grows quickly with features, so hierarchical FSMs or behavior trees are used to keep structure manageable.
q: A delivery robot's FSM has no transition out of WAIT_FOR_ELEVATOR if the elevator never arrives. What design fix best addresses this?
Merge WAIT_FOR_ELEVATOR with the DRIVE state to reduce state count
Replace the FSM with a learned policy trained on elevator rides
Make the robot re-enter WAIT_FOR_ELEVATOR more frequently
Add a timeout transition to a recovery or replanning state
A deadlock state needs an exit condition; a timeout transition to recovery is the standard fix. Re-entering the same state or merging states does not create an escape route.
fsm.t: Write a small Python FSM for a line-following robot with states FOLLOW, LOST, SEARCH, STOP using a dict of transitions; simulate a sequence of sensor events and print the state trajectory.

mdp.s: States, actions, transition probabilities, and rewards: the formal model of sequential decisions under uncertainty.
i: An MDP is (S, A, P, R, γ): states, actions, transition probabilities P(s' | s, a), reward R(s, a), and discount γ in [0, 1).
The Markov property means the next state depends only on the current state and action, so an optimal policy can be a function of the current state alone.
The objective is to maximize expected discounted return E[Σ γ^t r_t]; γ < 1 keeps infinite sums finite and trades off immediate versus future reward.
q: A robot's MDP state includes only its position, but its wheels sometimes slip depending on how fast it was moving. What modeling issue does this create?
The reward becomes undefined for states with slippage
The state is not Markov, since dynamics depend on hidden velocity
The discount factor must be set to 1 to compensate
The action space becomes continuous and cannot be modeled

If transitions depend on velocity not in the state, P(s' | s, a) is not well defined from position alone, breaking the Markov property; the fix is augmenting the state with velocity. Discounting does not address it.
mdp.t: Write a 3-state, 2-action MDP as NumPy arrays P[a, s, s'] and R[s, a]; check each row of P sums to 1 and compute the value of a fixed policy by solving V = R_π + γ P_π V.

dynamic_programming.s: Solve decisions backward in time through the principle of optimality. The same idea underlies LQR, shortest-path search, and value iteration.
i: Principle of optimality: the tail of an optimal policy is optimal for the tail subproblem, so costs can be computed backward from the final stage.
Finite horizon backward recursion: J_N(x) = terminal cost, J_k(x) = min_u [g(x, u) + E J_k+1(f(x, u, w))]; the minimizing u gives the optimal feedback policy at each stage.
The Bellman equation V*(s) = max_a [R(s, a) + γ Σ P(s'|s,a) V*(s')] is the infinite-horizon version; LQR and Dijkstra-style shortest path are special cases of this recursion.
q: Why does dynamic programming solve a finite-horizon problem backward from the final step rather than forward from the start?
The cost-to-go at each stage needs the optimal costs of later stages
Forward computation would violate the Markov property
Backward recursion avoids having to enumerate states
The terminal cost is unknown until the first step is taken
J_k is defined in terms of J_k+1, so you need the future optimal costs first, starting from the known terminal cost. DP still enumerates states, which is the curse of dimensionality.
dynamic_programming.t: On a 5-node directed graph with edge costs, compute shortest costs-to-go to a goal by backward DP by hand, then read off the optimal next node from every node.

value_policy_iteration.s: Iterative algorithms that compute the optimal value function and policy when the model is known.
i: Value iteration repeats V_k+1(s) = max_a [R(s, a) + γ Σ P(s'|s,a) V_k(s')]; the Bellman operator is a γ-contraction, so V_k converges to V* from any start.
Policy iteration alternates evaluation (solve V_π = R_π + γ P_π V_π exactly) and improvement (π(s) = argmax_a of the one-step lookahead), and terminates in finitely many iterations.
Both need the full model P and R; policy iteration usually needs few iterations but each is expensive, while value iteration has cheap iterations but may need many as γ approaches 1.
q: You raise the discount factor γ from 0.9 to 0.99 in value iteration. What happens to convergence?
It speeds up, since future rewards are weighted more strongly
It is unchanged, since convergence depends only on the state count
It slows down, since error shrinks by a factor γ per iteration
It stops converging, since the Bellman operator is no longer a contraction
The error bound shrinks by γ per sweep, so γ = 0.99 needs roughly 10 times more iterations than 0.9. It is still a contraction for any γ < 1.
value_policy_iteration.t: Implement value iteration on a 4x4 gridworld with a +1 goal and -0.04 step cost; count iterations to reach max change below 1e-6 for γ = 0.9 and γ = 0.99.

rl_fundamentals.s: Learn to act from trial and error when the dynamics model is unknown, trading off exploration and exploitation.
i: In RL the agent does not know P or R; it interacts with the environment, observing (s, a, r, s') tuples, and must learn a good policy from this experience.
Exploration versus exploitation: acting greedily on current estimates can miss better actions, so strategies like ε-greedy or optimism deliberately try uncertain actions.
Methods split into model-free (learn values or policies directly) and model-based (learn dynamics, then plan), and into on-policy versus off-policy depending on which policy generated the data.
q: An agent always takes the action with the highest current value estimate from the start, with values initialized to zero. What is the main risk?
Its value estimates will diverge to infinity
It will need a model of the transition probabilities
It will explore too much and never exploit
It may lock onto an early action and never find better ones

Pure greedy behavior never tests actions that look worse, so an early lucky outcome can trap it in a suboptimal choice. Divergence is a different issue, related to function approximation and off-policy bootstrapping.
rl_fundamentals.t: Simulate a 10-armed bandit with Gaussian rewards and compare average reward over 1000 steps for ε = 0, 0.01, and 0.1 using sample-average value estimates.

td_learning.s: Estimate values from sampled experience, either from full episodes or by bootstrapping from the next state's estimate.
i: Monte Carlo estimates V(s) by averaging complete returns G_t observed after visiting s; it is unbiased but has high variance and must wait until episode end.
TD(0) updates V(s) toward r + γ V(s') after each step: V(s) += α [r + γ V(s') - V(s)], bootstrapping from the current estimate of the next state.
TD learns online and has lower variance but is biased by its own estimates; n-step returns and TD(λ) interpolate between TD(0) and Monte Carlo.
q: A task has very long episodes and noisy rewards, and you need to update values during an episode. Which choice fits best and why?
Monte Carlo, because it is unbiased and the bias of TD would dominate
TD learning, because it updates every step and reduces variance
Monte Carlo, because it works without knowing the reward function
TD learning, because it requires no discount factor at all

TD updates online after each transition and its bootstrapped target has lower variance than full noisy returns. Monte Carlo must wait for episode end; both are model-free, so that is not a distinguishing factor.
td_learning.t: On the 5-state random walk (terminal reward 1 on the right), run MC and TD(0) for 100 episodes with α = 0.1 and compare RMS error against the true values 1/6, 2/6, ..., 5/6.

value_based_rl.s: Learn action values from experience and act greedily on them, scaling to large problems with function approximation.
i: Q-learning updates Q(s, a) += α [r + γ max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)]; it is off-policy, learning the greedy policy's values while behaving, e.g., ε-greedily.
With a tabular Q and enough exploration plus decaying step sizes, Q-learning converges to Q*, and the optimal policy is π(s) = argmax_a Q*(s, a).
Deep Q-networks approximate Q with a neural net, stabilized by experience replay and a slowly updated target network; the max operator also causes overestimation, which Double DQN reduces.
q: Why does DQN use a separate, slowly updated target network when computing r + γ max Q(s', a')?
To stop the regression target from shifting with every gradient step
To allow the algorithm to learn on-policy from fresh data only
To convert the problem into a supervised task with true labels
To remove the need for exploration through ε-greedy actions

If the same rapidly changing network defines the target, training chases a moving target and can oscillate or diverge; freezing it periodically stabilizes learning. The targets are still bootstrapped, not true labels.
value_based_rl.t: Implement tabular Q-learning on a 4x4 FrozenLake-style gridworld (deterministic) with ε-greedy exploration; print the greedy policy as arrows after 2000 episodes.

policy_gradient.s: Optimize a parameterized policy directly by gradient ascent on expected return, with a learned critic to reduce variance.
i: Policy gradient methods parameterize π_θ(a|s) and ascend J(θ) = E[Σ γ^t r_t] using ∇J = E[Σ_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t) G_t] (REINFORCE), which needs no dynamics model.
Subtracting a baseline b(s), such as V(s), from G_t leaves the gradient unbiased but lowers variance; using A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s) gives the advantage form.
Actor-critic methods learn a critic (e.g. V_w via TD) to estimate advantages for the actor; PPO and similar methods also limit the policy change per update for stability.
q: In REINFORCE, you subtract a state-dependent baseline b(s) from the return. What does this change?
It biases the gradient toward more conservative actions
It changes the optimal policy the method converges to
It removes the need to sample trajectories from the policy
It reduces gradient variance without introducing bias
E[∇ log π(a|s) b(s)] = 0 because the score function has zero mean, so the expected gradient is unchanged while variance drops. The objective and optimum are unaffected.
policy_gradient.t: For a 2-action softmax policy on a bandit with rewards 1 and 0, estimate the gradient with 1000 samples with and without a baseline of 0.5, and compare the means and variances.

model_based_rl.s: Learn a dynamics model from data and plan or control with it, connecting learning back to the control chapters.
i: Model-based RL fits a dynamics model x_t+1 ≈ f_θ(x_t, u_t) from data, e.g. by least squares for linear systems (system identification) or with neural nets, then plans or controls with it.
It is typically far more sample-efficient than model-free RL, since each transition trains a reusable model; planning can use MPC, iLQR, or simulated rollouts.
Model errors get exploited by the planner, which seeks regions where the model is wrong; ensembles, uncertainty estimates, short horizons, and replanning with new data mitigate this.
q: A planner using a learned dynamics model finds a plan that looks great in the model but fails on the real robot. What is the most likely reason?
The reward function was not differentiable with respect to actions
The discount factor was too small for the planning horizon
The planner exploited model errors in poorly covered states
Model-based methods cannot handle continuous action spaces
Optimizers push toward states where the learned model is inaccurate and overly optimistic; this model exploitation is the classic failure. Continuous actions are handled routinely, e.g. by MPC.
model_based_rl.t: Simulate x_t+1 = A x_t + B u_t + noise for a 2-D system with random inputs, then recover A and B by least squares on stacked [x_t, u_t] and compare with the truth for 20 and 200 samples.

behavior_cloning.s: Train a policy by supervised learning on expert demonstrations. Fast to set up, but errors compound once the robot drifts from what it saw.
i: Behavior cloning treats imitation as supervised learning: fit π_θ(a | s) to expert pairs (s, a) by minimizing a loss such as squared error or negative log-likelihood.
It needs no reward and no environment interaction during training, making it simple and data-efficient when demonstrations cover the states the policy will visit.
Multimodal demonstrations (e.g. passing an obstacle left or right) break a unimodal regressor, which averages them; mixture models, diffusion policies, or action discretization help.
q: Half the demonstrations steer left around a pole and half steer right. A behavior cloning policy trained with mean squared error does what at the pole?
Randomly picks left or right with equal probability each time
Averages the two and drives roughly straight into the pole
Refuses to act because the loss cannot be minimized
Always picks the side that appeared first in the dataset
MSE regression predicts the conditional mean, which for two symmetric modes is the middle, the worst choice. Sampling from modes requires a multimodal policy class, not plain MSE.
behavior_cloning.t: Create a dataset where s is in [-1, 1] and the action is +1 or -1 at random; fit a linear regressor and a 2-component mixture (or classifier) and compare predictions at s = 0.

covariate_shift.s: A cloned policy makes small errors, drifts into states the expert never showed, and errors compound. Understanding this explains most imitation learning failures and the fixes for them.
i: Training states come from the expert's distribution, but at test time the learner visits states induced by its own policy; small mistakes push it into states never seen in training.
Errors compound: with per-step error ε, behavior cloning's expected cost can grow like O(ε T²) over horizon T, versus O(ε T) when trained on the learner's own state distribution.
DAgger fixes this by rolling out the learner, having the expert label the visited states, aggregating the data, and retraining; noise injection during demos (DART) also broadens coverage.
q: A self-driving policy trained on perfect lane-centered human driving drifts off-center and then fails to recover. What fix addresses the root cause?
Train longer on the same demonstrations to lower training error
Use a bigger network so it can memorize every expert state
Increase the discount factor so future errors are penalized
Collect expert labels on states the learned policy itself visits

The problem is that off-center states are missing from training; DAgger-style relabeling of the learner's own states supplies recovery data. Lower training error on expert states does not cover new states.
covariate_shift.t: Simulate a 1-D lane-keeping task where the expert action is -k x; train a policy only on near-zero x, roll it out with small noise, and compare drift with a DAgger loop that adds expert-labeled visited states.

inverse_rl.s: Infer the reward an expert seems to be optimizing, then learn a policy for that reward.
i: Inverse RL assumes the expert is near-optimal for an unknown reward R and seeks an R under which the expert's behavior beats alternatives, then solves RL for that R.
The problem is ill-posed: many rewards (including R = 0) explain the same behavior, so methods add structure such as feature matching or the maximum entropy principle.
A learned reward can transfer to new dynamics or environments better than a cloned policy, but IRL is expensive since it typically solves an RL problem inside its loop.
q: Why might inverse RL generalize better than behavior cloning when the robot is deployed in a new environment layout?
The recovered reward captures goals, and replanning adapts to new dynamics
IRL does not need any demonstrations, so it avoids dataset bias
IRL produces a unique reward that is exactly the expert's true reward
IRL avoids solving any RL or planning problem during deployment

A reward encodes what the expert wants, so optimizing it in a new setting yields new appropriate behavior, while a cloned policy just maps states to actions seen before. IRL rewards are not unique, and it still needs demos and planning.
inverse_rl.t: In a 1-D chain of 5 states, write two different reward functions (including a shaped one) that both make 'always move right' optimal, illustrating why IRL is ill-posed.
